News.title: Secrets of iconic red despatch box that links Andy Burnham with Angelina Jolie
News.content:
The late Queen received one every day of her reign, Margaret Thatcher’s sold for almost a quarter of a million pounds and another rests at the home of Hollywood star Angelina Jolie. Now, as Andy Burnham settles into his new role as Prime Minister, he too will be the recipient of an iconic red despatch box.

For centuries the familiar lockable red cases have been used by British sovereigns, prime ministers and ministers to carry top secret documents and confidential papers. The boxes are interwoven with the history of Britain, containing information which has taken the country to war, ensured peace and shaped society.

Record label that made The Smiths spills 50 years of secrets READ MORE :

But Mohammed Suleman, the man behind the Barrow, Hepburn & Gale which produces the boxes, insists he doesn’t lie awake at night worrying about what they might contain. He laughs: “I worry more about what’s not being carried in them! There are rules in place about their use and strict protocols. They shouldn’t be ignored.”

View 4 Images King Charles III carrying out official government duties from his red box in the Eighteenth Century Room at Buckingham Palace (Image: BUCKINGHAM PALACE/AFP via Getty)

‌



The firm was founded back in 1760 when John Hepburn, a tanner from Yorkshire, moved to London and set up a tannery in Bermondsey - then a major centre for leather tanning. The business grew and expanded, merging with other manufacturers including one which already held the right to make despatch boxes for the British government.

Over the years, the company became one of Britain's largest leather manufacturers, their workers’ expertise being passed down the generations and even providing equipment for both World Wars. Field Marshall Montgomery visited the London factory ahead of the Allied invasion of Normandy, to meet the craftswomen who were making leather and canvas equipment crucial to the operation.

The heart of the company, though, remained the production of despatch boxes, with their red stained leather and gold print which has remained unchanged since Gladstone used one for his budget in 1853. Mr Suleman, who has previously worked in a business advisory capacity for UK companies, acquired the firm 26 years ago, after ploughing in private family money. At the time, there was both Russian and Chinese interest in the company.

View 4 Images Cherie Blair and Tony Blair, pictured in 2004 (Image: Dennis Stone/Shutterstock)

‌



He recalls: “It was a small box advert in the pink pages of the Financial Times. It read, ‘interesting prestige business for sale’ and mentioned signing a confidentiality agreement.

I didn’t understand why they were being so cagey, but when I picked through it all I realised that this was a significant business. Not only was it doing stuff that was centre stage but it was one of the country's oldest established suppliers to the military. There was a lot more going on beneath that simple advert.”

The boxes themselves are still made in a traditional way, in workshops situated across the country, the skills passed on down the years from worker to worker. Mr Suleman explains: “We try to use as many workshops around the country as we can. Many are family owned businesses on which we rely.

View 4 Images The Queen seated at her desk in her private audience room at Buckingham Palace with one of her official red boxes which she received almost every day of her reign, containing important papers from government ministers (Image: PA)

‌



“We try to do our bit because without some of the crucial support that we provide these skills would be lost. We’ve been here for a long time as a business but sadly I think short-termism is a disease which has affected this country for a number of years. That’s not how we operate here. Politicians need to walk around the shop floor and get their hands dirty.”

He won’t disclose how many boxes are made in a year - he says demand is determined by how active a government is - or how much one costs to make. No two boxes are the same though, with those privately commissioned - like the one Angelina Jolie has - varying in price.

He explains: “They can be very personalised so costs do vary. We made one for a collector of vintage watches, another to house a collection of pens."

News.title: 'I plunged into a freezing pool to find out just how deadly cold water shock can be'
News.content:
'I plunged into a freezing pool to find out just how deadly cold water shock can be'

EXCLUSIVE: The Mirror visited the University of Portsmouth’s Extreme Environments Lab to learn more about the potentially deadly effects of cold water shock

The Mirror takes a cold plunge

As temperatures continue to soar this week, thousands of us will be heading to beaches, lakes and rivers to cool off.

‌



But while it’s hot on land, the water remains very cold – and can easily cause you to drown. We visited the University of Portsmouth’s Extreme Environments Lab to learn more about the potentially deadly effects of cold water shock.

‌



Wired up to a heart monitor and breathing tube, I spent 10 minutes in a specialist plunge pool set at 15C – the current, average UK sea temperature. The room was heated to 28C to mimic the heat we’re seeing during the current heatwave.

‌



View 5 Images Saskia's gasp increased to 1.5 litres on entering the cold water (Image: Tim Merry/Staff Photographer)

Before entering the water, my gasp rate – the amount of oxygen breathed in – was a normal 0.3 litres. But on being lowered into the pool, this rocketed to 1.5 litres – which shockingly, if my face was under water, would be enough to drown me.

My heart rate also shot up – going from a normal, resting, 80 beats per minute to 110. This sudden change causes the blood vessels to constrict, which can trigger a heart or cardiac arrest, even in young people. Cold water shock, causing the gasp response or heart failure, accounts for around 60% of drownings.

‌



Spending time in cold water also impacts our dexterity. Before getting in, I was able to type the text “Get me out of here” in just two seconds. But after 10 minutes in the water, it took me eight seconds to write the same message.

View 5 Images Saskia's heart rate increased from 80 beats per minute to 110 (Image: Tim Merry/Staff Photographer)

Infrared cameras were also used to show my body heat before and after immersion. Before, I was covered in yellow, which indicates body heat, but afterwards turned almost entirely blue.

‌



I also tried out the pool’s flume feature, which creates a strong current. Despite being a regular and strong swimmer, battling against the force of the cold water for just three minutes left me exhausted and out of breath.

The University of Portsmouth’s Professor Mike Tipton, the UK’s leading expert on extreme environments, said: “Cold shock is initiated by a rapid fall in skin temperature on initial immersion - this stimulates cold receptors just below the surface of the skin.

View 5 Images Professor Mike Tipton is urging swimmers to stay within a safe depth

‌



“If at any time the airway is submerged when breathing is out of control people can inhale water and drown. At the same time the cold shock response includes an increase in blood pressure and cardiac workload. Cold shock also makes it hard to co-ordinate swim stroke and breathing and can lead to early swim failure.”

Urging the public to stay vigilant, Prof Tipton, who began investigating cold water shock in the 1980s, added: “Swim parallel to the shore and stay in your depths, be aware that your swimming ability in a warm indoor swimming pool does not relate to your swimming ability in open cold water. Tides, currents, windage and cold can easily turn a ‘swimmer’ into a ‘non-swimmer.”

Prof Tipton’s stark warning comes after at least 26 people - mainly children and young people - drowned in the heatwaves in May and June. The Mirror ’s Save Lives for Sam campaign was launched after an unprecedented 19 people lost their lives in water in May alone. We’re pushing for change in memory of 16-year-old Sam Haycock, who drowned in a reservoir in Rotherham, South Yorks, during hot weather on his last day of school in 2021.

‌



View 5 Images Sam Haycock drowned in a reservoir aged 16 (Image: Haycock family)

The UK is currently in the midst of its third heatwave in just two months, with temperatures set to hit 34C in some areas on Saturday. Amber heat health alerts have been issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) for the Midlands and southern England until 9pm on Sunday. The alert means significant impacts are likely across health and social care services.

The RNLI urges anyone who gets into difficulty to practice the ‘Float to Live” technique. The charity’s water safety manager Ross Macleod said: "The key thing for floating is learning to relax in the water, tilt your head back with your ears submerged, and control your breathing.

‌



View 5 Images The Mirror's Save Lives For Sam campaign is calling on the government to take water safety seriously

"Don't worry if your legs sink, as we all float differently. Practice in a supervised location to learn what floating looks and feels like for you.”

If you’re on shore and see someone getting into difficulty, the National Water Safety Forum urges people to use the ‘Phone, Float Throw’ method – call the emergency services, tell the person to float and throw them something buoyant like a water bottle or life ring.

Article continues below

The Mirror has launched the Save Lives For Sam water safety campaign to tackle the UK's growing drowning crisis. Backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families, the campaign is calling for urgent action to make our waters safer.

That includes compulsory water safety lessons in schools, a nationwide public awareness campaign, better lifesaving equipment at high-risk waterways, the introduction of Sam's Law, and a dedicated Minister for Water Safety. Find out more about the campaign and how you can support it here.

News.title: Ben Needham’s grandfather dies without the answers he spent decades seeking
News.content:
Ben Needham’s grandfather dies without the answers he spent decades seeking

EXCLUSIVE: Missing Ben Needham's mum Kerry told the Mirror: "My dad never ever agreed with the police theory there had been an accident. He believed Ben was abducted"

View 7 Images Ben Needham's grandad has died aged 77 (Image: Daily Mirror)

Ben Needham's grandfather has tragically died on the eve of the 35th anniversary of his grandson’s disappearance.

‌



Ben’s mum Kerry Needham, 54, who now lives in Turkey, said: “We’re all devastated. About a month ago he said to me; ‘I’m tired, I’ve had enough but I don’t want to go without knowing what’s happened to Ben’.

‌



“He held on as long as he could. It has tormented him for 35 years. Will he rest in peace? I don’t think he will, not until we know what happened.

‌



Kerry added: “My dad never ever agreed with the police theory there had been an accident. He believed Ben was abducted. Once I have the strength back from this, I am now even more determined to fight for the answers that my dad longed for.”

7 View 7 Images Ben Needham disappeared on the island of Kos (Image: Press Association) 7 View 7 Images He disappeared 35 years ago (Image: Mirrorpix)

‌



Kerry was told her dad died on Thursday, just hours before the harrowing anniversary of her son’s disappearance from the island of Kos. Ben was 21 months old when he went missing on July 24 1991.

Her mum Christine was babysitting and had taken the toddler to see grandad Eddie, who was renovating a farmhouse on the island at the time. Eddie, 77, a former builder from Sheffield, South Yorkshire, was a grandad-of-four and great-grandad to two, and was married to wife Christine.

He had suffered from cancer recently but had recovered after treatment. The family were left in shock after he took a turn for the worse during a day out with his son Stephen.

‌



Kerry said: “He was a strong, hardworking family man, who could be very funny and sarcastic. He didn’t suffer fools gladly. He was a very good judge of character. He had a really good sense of humour and he was always telling jokes.

View 7 Images Kerry found out about Eddie's death on Thursday this week (Image: Daily Mirror)

“But when it came to Ben he was very very serious. He would take the lead on my behalf, talking to the authorities. He would do anything for his family. He went everywhere looking for Ben. He would sleep on the beach to save money on hotel rooms when his health was okay.

‌



“But he lived with an awful lot of guilt. I tried to convince him that I never blamed him or my mum. I wanted that pain of that guilt to stop but there was nothing I could ever say to him that would stop it, he lived with it every day until he died.”

Talking about how her parents ended up living in Kos, Kerry said: “He loved travelling and seeing different parts of the world. That changed my mindset too. It put it in my blood. I wanted the same adventures as they were having. That’s why I followed them to Kos.”

During his last visit to the island of Kos, Eddie spoke to the Mirror about the immense guilt he lived with for persuading Kerry to join them in Greece with Ben. He broke down sobbing as he approached the farmhouse where Ben was last seen and cried: “I hate this place. I hate this place. I can't take any more.”

‌



View 7 Images Family members initially believed Ben disappeared as locals became concerned for his wellbeing (Image: Daily Mirror)

He told us how he would dream of his grandson Ben on Kos, pleading: "Please come and find me, Grandad, I'm here."

He said: "The biggest thing that's haunted me is, I used to hear him in my head, 'I'm here, Grandad. Come and find me, I'm here'. I searched everywhere; the ravine, the brambles, the outbuildings, the well.

‌



"I had to give up searching for Ben for my own sanity. It was sending me mad. I couldn't think or operate properly."

Eddie and his wife Christine, fell in love with Kos during their first holiday abroad together in September 1990 and quickly made the decision to sell up in Sheffield and move to their island haven. Shop worker Christine, then 37, and builder Eddie, 39, sold their home and bought a caravan for the 2,340 mile journey with their two youngest, Stephen, then 17 and Danny, 11. The four set off at the end of December 1990 sending regular updates back home to new mum Kerry.

Eddie recalled: "When we got to Kos we had a great life at first, fishing all the time, catching octopus and eels and cooking them. We thought, 'What a life!'"

‌



View 7 Images Eddie said he would often dream about his grandson and the disappearance (Image: Daily Mirror)

After reading letters about their wonderful life overseas, Kerry, living in a council flat in Sheffield, soon decided to join them with their first grandchild, Ben. They had been hoping for a fantastic life together in Greece, but it turned into a nightmare.

On the morning of July 24, 1991, Kerry went to work and Christine and Danny pushed Ben in a pushchair for the half-an-hour trip to visit the farmhouse. It was the tot's first trip there to see his grandad Eddie and uncle Stephen working, while a digger driver moved rubble from a different property down the lane.

‌



It was only after work had finished for the day that it became apparent Ben was missing. Eddie said: "The last time I saw Ben he was playing just outside. He had a stick and was poking the mud and throwing water over himself. For some reason I thought Danny was outside with him but Danny said he was inside eating."

View 7 Images An age progression facial depiction of what Ben Needham would look like today (Image: Andy Commins / Daily Mirror)

Several witnesses claim to have seen a strange car in the lane at the time of Ben’s disappearance. After searching frantically, they called the police and Eddie had the devastating duty to tell Kerry they could not find her son.

‌



He recalled: "I had to stand and watch as police got a JCB and tipped the pile of building dirt from the site next door very slowly. Every bucketful felt as if my guts were falling out.

"They moved the dirt from A to B, and police expected Ben’s body to roll out. Then they moved it back again. There was never a proper investigation or a proper search. It was never treated as a crime scene.

"There was a man from the BBC based in Athens at the time and he said he could try and get heatseeking equipment from the UK to search but the police officer in charge said 'no' because he didn't think Ben was on the island.

Article continues below

"He said the birds would have alerted them as they come in huge numbers even if a small animal is dead. He said the ground was too hard for someone to have buried him.

"I feel so much guilt. I still blame myself," Eddie said. "If we hadn't persuaded Kerry to join us with Ben this would never have happened and he would still be with us."

Kerry added: "I am determined to find the answers so my dad can rest in peace."

News.title: Inside No10 North as Andy Burnham sets up his new power base
News.content:
Inside No10 North as Andy Burnham sets up his new power base

Heron House in Manchester is now home to No10 North - a stark contrast to the cramped corridors and offices of 10 Downing Street which has been home to British PMs since the 18th Century

View 3 Images Andy Burnham worked from No10 North in Manchester for the first time on Friday (Image: James Speakman/The Times/PA Wire)

For centuries, there has only been one No10.

‌



The Downing Street townhouse, which has been home to British Prime Ministers since 1735, is famous around the world and a symbol of prime ministerial power. But now there's a second black door - in an office block in Manchester.

‌



Andy Burnham plans to turn Heron House, the north-west base for security agency GCHQ, into Britain's nerve centre, in a statement move to show he means business when he promised to stamp out regional inequalities plaguing Britain.

‌



Opportunities to look inside have been rare in recent years due to the top-secret work carried out within its walls. But Mr Burnham threw open the doors to cameras on Friday, offering a glimpse of the office from where the country will be run - for one day a week at least.

Angela Rayner rules out rent controls as she admits 1.5million home pledge getting harder to meet READ MORE :

View 3 Images Andy Burnham is welcomed to the new office (Image: James Speakman/The Times/PA Wire)

A replica No10 door stands in the entrance to greet visitors, with glass-fronted office rooms printed with the image of the Manchester worker bee - an image Mr Burnham has tattooed on his arm.

‌



Portraits by Stanley Chow, who created the artwork used in Mr Burnham's Makerfield by-election campaign, are dotted around of famous Mancunians such as footballer Marcus Rashford, mathematician Alan Turing, suffragette Emmeline Pankhurst and poet Lemn Sissay.

Mr Burnham will know the building well, having been Mayor of Greater Manchester for nearly a decade. Standing in an open space with a patterned grey, brown and cream floor and large windows looking out onto Albert Square, he described it as a "full circle moment".

It marks a stark contrast to the historic grandeur of 10 Downing Street. But despite the lavish surroundings, its occupants have long complained about the challenges of working behind the famous black door.

‌



View 3 Images The PM and his wife Marie-France van Heel being welcomed into Downing Street on Monday (Image: Kin Cheung/PA Wire)

Teams are siloed off in different parts of the building, connected by a maze of corridors. Staff are crammed into tiny offices while massive state rooms are infrequently used.

Keir Starmer joked to friends that he would open a door to what he thought was a cupboard and find a room full of people.

Article continues below

Despite the presence of veteran No10 cat Larry, mice can be spotted running between desks. Aides said the air con and heating can be patchy and the cold taps sometimes run lukewarm, while food has to be brought over from the neighbouring Cabinet Office canteen.

One No10 official said: "It's a higgledy-piggledy building that's really not a modern work place."

News.title: Iran war timer ticking down as Donald Trump weighs up 'all-out war' with ground troops on Kharg Island
News.content:
Iran war timer ticking down as Donald Trump weighs up 'all-out war' with ground troops on Kharg Island

US President Donald Trump is losing patience with Iran and has moved a staggering amount of war machinery, including squadrons of fighter bombers, heavy bombers, special forces and medics

View 3 Images US forces launch precision strikes in latest round of Iran attacks (Image: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP via Getty Images)

US forces hit Iran hard in a 13th consecutive night of attacks amid growing concern in America’s military that President Donald Trump will escalate the war this weekend.

‌



All week the US has surged its military hardware in the region with extra squadrons of fighter planes and defensive batteries moved into position, along with extra weapons. More Special Forces have been flown into the area and on Friday at least 10 KC-135R Stratotankers flew from the US to stop off at Israeli bases to refuel.

‌



These large-scale warplanes are used to perform perilous air-to-air refuelling of the US air force and navy fighter bombers on long-range missions. Two B-1B Lancer strategic bombers flew from RAF Fairford to an unknown location in readiness for a green-light to launch a major assault on Iran. A large contingent of medics has also been moved up into position in readiness for a flood of casualties if full-scale war does break out.

‌



View 3 Images US President Donald Trump decides on war (Image: Getty Images)

Iran in horror threat to UK and chilling warning to Royal Family READ MORE :

It came in the wake of threats from the Iranian regime against Fairford for having hosted the B1 Bombers, Tehran claiming they launched from the Gloucestershire base. President Trump has warned he may order a large-scale rise in tempo of the conflict this weekend and sources say it is looking likely he will go -ahead.

‌



One told the Mirror: “There is increasing concern that Trump will escalate this weekend. It is very possible this may involve some kind of ground incursion. Both Trump and so-called Secretary of War Pete Hegseth had a terrible week because of the lack of mission clarity and strategy and there has been no shift in attitude from the Iranians.

“Trump may do it to distract from his various issues and Hegseth because he has a deranged sense of masculinity and is obsessed with displaying US military power. But taking the fight to Iran will not be popular.”

View 3 Images US precision strikes on Iranian military targets (Image: US Central Command (CENTCOM)/AFP via Getty Images)

Article continues below

One possibility is that the US will decide to occupy Kharg Island, off the coast of Iran, which holds a dominant position to control the safety of ships in the Strait of Hormuz. But it would require an invasion force of thousands of US Marines, vehicles, helicopters and transport planes to conduct such an enormous operation. The looming attack alert went up as Iran’s proxy fighting forces in the region also became increasingly involved in the conflict.

Pro-Iranian Iraqi militia unit Awliya al-Dam claims it attacked Jordan, Kuwait and Saudi Arabia as the Houthis step up threats to shipping in the Red Sea. Israel is on alert for the US stepping up its attacks after Mossad foiled an Iranian plot to infiltrate proxy operatives into Israel to kill senior officials. Israeli intelligence says Iran is using ‘proxy by proxy’ hiring of criminals now to launch foreign attacks. According to Mossad Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence and Security (MOIS) was behind the plot.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
News.content:
A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".

Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.

On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.

Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers.

"In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He added: "We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort.

"We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."

The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.

Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

He continued: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

A lawyer for the families of the attack's survivors said they did not want to give "notoriety" to Rudakubana and that attention should be focused on supporting the children around the anniversary.

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly of Fletchers Solicitors said: "The focus of public outrage should not be on moves that this perpetrator has made, it should be examining how we are two years on from this attack and some of these girls are still not receiving the proper psychological care and support that they should be to recover from this."

Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions.

The court also heard how Rudakubana presented as having high functioning autism and did not have any associated learning disabilities.

Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13, adding: "However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."

Rudakubana was deemed mentally fit to be detained, interviewed and stand trial. His late guilty plea meant his mental health was not discussed in detail in court during a trial.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

News.title: 'Extremely significant' bomb in car intercepted on way to NI, Irish police say
News.content:
A car containing an "extremely significant" bomb has been intercepted in the Republic of Ireland as it was being driven across the border for an attack in Northern Ireland, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) have said.

The vehicle was stopped in County Monaghan on Wednesday during an operation targeting dissident republican activities.

BBC News NI understands police in Northern Ireland's main theory is that the bomb was set to be used to attack a police station north of the border.

A woman in her 20s has been charged and is due to appear in court in County Meath on Friday evening, while a man in his 40s remains in custody.

Police sources in Northern Ireland believe the New IRA was likely responsible.

The vehicle was stopped on the N2 near Carrickmacross at about 15:00 on Wednesday.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed on Friday that officers had found an explosive device.

Irish broadcaster RTÃ reported that gardaÃ­ sources said the bomb contained a power unit, a detonator and military grade explosives.

News.title: Officers hurt as police boat hits Westminster Bridge
News.content:
Five Metropolitan Police officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London.

The Met said the incident occurred at about 15:40 BST and involved a boat from the Marine Policing Unit which was carrying armed officers.

In a statement, it said "a number of officers entered the water, but were recovered" adding it was waiting for an "update on the extent of their injuries".

No members of the public are thought to have been involved or injured in the crash.

Officers who had been recovered from the river were seen being treated by paramedics on a rigid black inflatable boat moored to the side of the river.

Members of the public have been cleared from the area and a large number of police officers, fire crews and ambulances are at the scene.

A cordon has been placed either end of the bridge, which crosses the River Thames next to the Houses of Parliament, and buses and coaches travelling on it were forced to reverse and find another route.

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters".

"Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?
News.content:
Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.

He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.

BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about Â£1.5bn.

Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line.

News.title: NBA superstar LeBron James to join Philadelphia 76ers
News.content:
LeBron James has announced he will be joining the Philadelphia 76ers next season for what he says will be his final contract in the NBA.

The 41-year-old, the highest points scorer in the history of the league, left the Los Angeles Lakers after eight years last month.

The Cleveland Cavaliers, Golden State Warriors, Minnesota Timberwolves and Miami Heat were also rumored to be in the running for the four-time NBA champion.

"I believe I can help make the Philadelphia 76ers a championship team and I am so excited to energise a new fanbase and start this incredible journey one last time," James said on X., external

Earlier this week, James' former team Miami mistakenly posted a link to an 'introductory press conference' for James.

A Heat spokesperson told Reuters, external the video was posted in error by staff who were preparing for the possibility of James rejoining the team he won two NBA titles with in 2012 and 2013.

Either side of that, James had two spells with Cleveland, who drafted James in 2003 and are based near his hometown of Akron, Ohio.

"Miami I'll forever love and Northeast Ohio will always [be] home," James added.

More to follow.

News.title: Four men dead after car crashes into lamp-post
News.content:
Four men have died after a car hit a lamp-post on Merseyside, police have said.

The car left the road and crashed on Liverpool Road, Huyton, just before 02:00 BST.

The men, two aged 23, and two others, aged 24 and 26 died at the scene, Merseyside Police said.

A 27-year-old man who was a passenger inside the vehicle has been taken to hospital and is in a stable condition, the force added.

The black Seat Cupra had been travelling from Liverpool towards Knowsley before it came off the road and hit the lamp-post.

Eleven roads in the area have been closed, including Liverpool Road and East Prescot Road, from the junction of Princess Drive and Finch Lane while police carry out their investigations.

News.title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
News.content:
It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.

From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.

Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.

Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.

These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.

In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.

The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.

What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.

While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.

The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.

At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).

It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.

The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.

The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.

This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.

News.title: Mega dinghy carries record 165 migrants to UK
News.content:
A record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat, the Home Office has confirmed.

The number broke the previous record from July, when 128 crossed the Channel from France in one vessel.

Border Security Command was pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on Thursday afternoon.

A Home Office spokesperson said the crossing served as a "stark reminder that criminal gangs have no regard for the safety of those they claim to help".

"The reality is clear and lives are being lost in the Channel," they added.

A total of 162 people died, external in the busy waterway between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.

This rises to 257 when considering other migration-related deaths in the area, such as accidents involving people trying to board lorries bound for the UK, it added.

News.title: Fifty women tell BBC they were pressured into having sex with strangers
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have told the BBC they were pressured or coerced by their partners into having sex with strangers.

They got in contact following an investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 people she did not know.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex through swinging despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

News.title: Chris Mason: What Burnham's first week in power tells us about his agenda
News.content:
"We are on borrowed time if we don't get a move on," Angela Rayner, the former deputy prime minister who is back in the cabinet this week as housing secretary, told the BBC's Today programme on Friday.

It has been quite the week at Westminster. Sir Keir Starmer's departure as prime minister on Monday seems rather a while ago.

The fledgling Burnham administration has been seeking to find its feet and make a decent first impression at the same time, as many try to do in the first days in a job.

There has been an early pattern in these early days: an early morning nugget of news dropping from No10.

On Thursday, it was business rates in England; on Wednesday, it was bus fares in England and on Tuesday, it was a VAT cut on electricity bills.

Today, the prime minister is assembling what Rayner calls "a pride of mayors" among others for a meeting of what is known as the National Economic Council at the new No10 North in Manchester.

Andy Burnham claims his new base in Manchester represents the beginning of "the biggest rebalancing of power our country has seen, external" and he will be "bringing forward the biggest changes in the last 40 years".

His early announcements have been considerably more piecemeal than that â he says his "10 year plan for Britain" will come later in the year.

It is worth remembering there was talk from both Boris Johnson and his allies and from Sir Keir Starmer about their plans for the decade ahead â both fizzled out rather more quickly than that.

So how should we assess how much politics has changed, or not?

The early evidence - and let's be frank, it is only that given we are just a few days in - points to Andy Burnham being both more sharp and more nimble than his predecessor in setting out what he is attempting to do and trying to point to early examples of what that might look like, with the announcements of the last few days.

With the tinkering of how the government is run, like the creation of the Office of Prime Minister, and the establishment of No 10 North, he's made it clear that the arteries of power flow very much to and from him.

He hopes he can overcome the critique of Sir Keir Starmer and others, that one of the frustrations of being prime minister can be pulling levers and nothing actually happens.

News.title: Chris Brown pleads guilty to affray over nightclub attack in London
News.content:
US singer Chris Brown has pleaded guilty to affray over what prosecutors called "a vicious and unprovoked attack" in a London nightclub in 2023.

Police said CCTV showed that Brown, one of the world's biggest R&B stars, hit the victim on the head with a glass bottle several times, and that the man was then chased, pushed to the floor and kicked.

The 37-year-old star had been due to face a trial on more serious charges, which he denied - assault, attempting to cause grievous bodily harm, and having an offensive weapon, namely a tequila bottle. However, those charges have now been dropped.

Affray, which is defined as using or threatening violence towards someone and making them fear for their safety, is punishable by up to three years in jail. Brown will be sentenced in October.

News.title: Hero swimmer helped two children during beach tragedy
News.content:
Witnesses say a heroic day-tripper managed to haul two children back to shore during an incident where a mother and daughter drowned.

Beverly Smit, 60, described the unnamed rescuer swimming out to sea three times as the tragedy unfolded in West Mersea, near Colchester, on Wednesday evening.

Shally Rahman, 41, and Samiha Rahman, 15, were trying to rescue a seven-year-old boy from the water when they got into difficulty and died.

Essex Police said the group, from Barking, east London, were all related to each other and the boy remained in hospital, fighting for his life.

Recalling the moment the "Good Samaritan" sprang into action, Smit said: "They were calling for help and the children and adults were out there.

"He swam out, I think, three times. Two of the children he brought back were not in good condition.

"It's not an easy swim when the tide's coming in - you're swimming against the tide. The water [on Wednesday] was particularly quite cold."

News.title: Heat health alerts in effect for parts of UK as rain returns for some this weekend
News.content:
Yellow heat health alerts came into effect across central and southern England on Friday morning with temperatures forecast to reach 30C (86F) in places.

The alerts, issued by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), cover the East and West Midlands, eastern England, London, south-east England and south-west England and are valid from 09:00 BST on Friday until 09:00 on Sunday.

The UKHSA warns that heat is expected to cause minor impacts for health and social care services, with an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

It comes as parts of the UK prepare to see much-needed rain this weekend - although amounts are expected to be relatively small, especially in the south.

A drought was officially declared for large parts of north and mid-Wales on Thursday.

The rest of Wales, along with much of central, southern and eastern England, is in "prolonged dry weather" category - one stage below a drought - and the Sottish Environment Protection Agency said much of eastern Scotland has moved into 'water scarcity' status

Hosepipe bans are in force for millions of the customers across eastern and southern England.

News.title: Dad who murdered four-week-old son jailed for 18 years
News.content:
A man who murdered his four-week-old son after drinking up to nine pints of beer on a night out has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Tony Bartlett returned to the family home in Chard, Somerset, on 16 July 2022 and shook baby Atticus in what the sentencing judge described as "a sudden fit of anger".

The 39-year-old caused serious injuries to his son's spinal cord and ribs, as well as brain damage so severe he never regained consciousness or the ability to breathe independently. Atticus died seven days later.

Bartlett, who was convicted after a trial at Bristol Crown Court earlier this month, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Warning: This story contains details which readers may find distressing.

The trial heard the former postman, from Axminster in Devon, had gone to a pub and comedy club with his then-partner Evelyn Ballentyne on the night Atticus was fatally injured.

It was their first evening out since their son's birth.

After they returned home, Ballentyne went upstairs and left Bartlett alone to feed Atticus.

News.title: Sarah Ferguson's charity formally closes down
News.content:
Sarah Ferguson's charity, Sarah's Trust, has formally wound up and is marked as "removed" on the public register of charities.

The charity said in February it would close "for the foreseeable future" days after new details emerged about the former Duchess of York's friendship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Among more than three million documents released by the US Department of Justice (DoJ) earlier this year were emails appearing to show Ferguson was in contact with Epstein while he was in prison for soliciting sex from a minor. Being named in the documents does not indicate wrongdoing.

The BBC has contacted Ferguson's representatives for comment on the closure of her charity.

Established in 2020, Sarah's Trust was "dedicated to supporting frontline, grassroots work to address the humanitarian and environmental crisis, the hunger crisis and issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty", according to its website.

In February, a spokesperson for the foundation said the decision to close had come after "some months" of discussion.

The foundation did not provide further details behind its decision to close at the time.

The massive drop of files by the DoJ earlier this year suggested Ferguson had been closer to Epstein than previously thought.

In the files, Ferguson was seen praising the late sex offender in 2009 as "the brother I have always wished for".

The emails also suggest she took her daughters along for lunch with him in Miami, days after his release from prison.

Ferguson's representatives have not responded to previous requests for comment on the documents.

The former duchess has already been dropped by multiple charities over her Epstein links.

In October, she lost her duchess title when her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, relinquished his Duke of York title over his links with Epstein, and she was also forced to move out of his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge, where the couple lived together, despite having divorced in 1996.

The Energy Department’s announcement of a civilian nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia triggered confusion and anger inside the White House, prompting a last-minute stipulation that has cast uncertainty over the deal’s future, according to a new report.

The agreement, years in the making, would allow Saudi Arabia to build nuclear reactors using U.S. technology. Energy Secretary Chris Wright and Saudi Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman signed it in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday alongside a bilateral safeguards agreement.

“Together, these two agreements lay the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar partnership that advances several priority economic and strategic objectives, including nuclear nonproliferation,” the Energy Department said in a news release.

However, President Donald Trump was unaware the deal was being announced, leading him and other staffers to become “livid,” according to CNN, which cited sources familiar with the matter.

Although the administration had been working on the agreement for months, the White House had asked the department not to unveil it on Wednesday, one source told the outlet. Wright proceeded with the announcement anyway.

open image in gallery The Energy Department’s announcement of a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia triggered panic inside the White House, according to a new report ( Getty Images )

Representatives for both the White House and Energy Department forcefully disputed that there was any misalignment.

“President Trump’s energy team is fully aligned, and always has been: the civil nuclear deal being brokered between the United States and Saudi Arabia is contingent on Saudi Arabia joining the successful Abraham Accords, which will help bring true peace to the Middle East,” White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told CNN.

“This is fake news. The Department of Energy has closely coordinated the negotiations and then announcement of these agreements with the White House and the State Department,” a department spokesperson told the outlet.

The Republican president’s anger intensified after conservative media outlets began criticizing the deal, sources told CNN. A Fox News host questioned whether the agreement would include a requirement that Saudi Arabia join the Abraham Accords, the deal forged during Trump’s first term that led several Arab states to normalize relations with Israel.

Experts on nonproliferation also expressed concern over the agreement’s enrichment provisions and its failure to commit to enhanced Additional Protocol safeguards.

open image in gallery Trump’s post post surprised the Saudi officials, who had not signed on to the requirement of normalization with Israel, according to CNN . Pictured: Crown Prince and Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia Mohammed bin Salman and Trump speak during the US-Saudi Investment Forum at the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts on November 19, 2025. ( AFP via Getty Images )

Following heavy criticism, Trump on Thursday wrote on Truth Social that the deal would be “totally subject to Saudi Arabia joining the very respected and successful Abraham Accords.” He added: “There will be no enrichment of material!”

The post surprised the Saudi officials, who had not signed on to the requirement of normalization, according to CNN.

But according to some Trump staffers, the deal—though signed—was not finalized because “letters required to be sent to Congress hadn’t gone out,” the outlet reported. The agreement is subject to congressional review, with a 90-day consideration period.

Sources close to the administration suspect the agreement, now in limbo, may have been subject to intervention by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters this week that, to her knowledge, Netanyahu and Trump had not spoken.

Tadej Pogacar conquered the famed hairpins of the Alpe d’Huez in a record time as he won stage 19 of the Tour de France to extend his overall lead.

Pogacar was timed at 35 minutes and 27 seconds over the 13.8km climb, smashing the previous record of 36 minutes 55 seconds set by Marco Pantani in 1997.

In the process, Pogacar became only the second man to win in yellow on this mountain following Geraint Thomas in 2018, taking his fifth stage win of this Tour and the 26th of his career.

The Slovenian took flight on the first of the hairpins and reeled in the remnants of a huge breakaway, closing a gap of three and a half minutes to catch final survivors Richard Carapaz and Lenny Martinez with 1.8km to go before dropping them inside the final 1,000 metres.

It saw Pogacar extend his overall lead to seven minutes 11 seconds over Remco Evenepoel, who himself attacked inside the last four kilometres to strengthen his grip on second.

“It’s very cool to win up here,” Pogacar said. “It was a crazy, crazy atmosphere all climb and it was thanks to all the team that I could pull it off. In the end I was riding for the team-mates today and I’m super happy to take the win…

“In the first kilometre (of the climb) I knew I had good legs and there’s not many guys left that can follow or try to go with me so I tried, then I committed to the top.”

He hardly needed to add any extra time to his lead to get closer to what would be a record-equalling fifth Tour de France title, but was determined to add his name to the esteemed list of riders who have won on the 32 occasions the Tour has visited this mountain since Fausto Coppi was the first in 1952.

Rival teams began the day wondering if Pogacar might be dealing with a hidden illness, having lost team-mate Brandon McNulty on Thursday while Adam Yates suffered hugely over the past two days.

open image in gallery There was speculation that Tadej Pogacar was dealing with a hidden illness ( Reuters )

Another team-mate, Tim Wellens, was suffering on Friday but Pogacar never looked troubled and Yates had recovered enough to get in the early break and offer his leader a big turn early on the Alpe.

What had been a break of more than 40 riders began to fracture after Mads Pedersen picked up maximum points at the intermediate sprint late on the 128km stage from Gap, and the break was still 14 strong when they arrived at the foot of the climb.

It was down to three – Carapaz, Martinez and Sepp Kuss – where the crowds parted and barriers began four kilometres from the summit, but Pogacar could see his prey.

As Kuss faded, Pogacar’s first attempt to drop Carapaz and Martinez failed but a second dig did the job as Pogacar won by six seconds from Martinez, who moved up to fifth overall.

Tom Pidcock, stage winner here in 2022, fell back early on the climb but battled to finish 20th on the stage, keeping him ninth overall with one mountain stage – on the other side of the Alpe on Saturday – left before Paris.

Massive forest fires are raging across southwestern France and central Spain, forcing the evacuation of an estimated 80,000 people from their homes. In France, some residents were compelled to flee by boat as flames engulfed the popular Cap Ferret peninsula on the Atlantic coast.

The blaze near Cap Ferret, located just 60 kilometres (37 miles) from Bordeaux, has consumed approximately 100 square kilometres (38 square miles) since Wednesday. This area, usually celebrated for its stunning landscapes, sandy beaches, oyster-farming villages, and upmarket resorts, is now under severe threat. Over 60,000 French residents have been displaced.

Both France and Spain have appealed to fellow European Union member states for urgent assistance to combat the escalating infernos.

open image in gallery Firefighters work to extinguish flames during a wildfire in Lege-Cap-Ferret in the Gironde department, amongst worsening drought conditions following a heatwave and water shortages across much of France. ( Reuters )

Hundreds of French firefighters have been deployed and additional ground and aerial reinforcements were sent Friday to tackle the blaze. Meanwhile, another major wildfire burned further south down the coast. It remained uncontained as strong winds did not help firefighters.

Authorities believe the cause of both fires was accidental.

France’s Interior minister, Laurent Nunez, said 40,000 people have been evacuated in the Gironde department, and 23,000 in the Landes.

French President Emmanuel Macron said France will receive EU reinforcements including two Croatian Canadair firefighting aircraft, two Portuguese Air Tractor aircraft, and two heavy-lift Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia. Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said that Italy and Greece are each sending two Canadair water-dumping airplanes.

The Clouds became ‘Darker and darker’

In southwest France, authorities sent boats to help the evacuation and a total of about 63,000 people, many of them tourists, were told to get out as two major, separate fires threatened homes and campsites, officials said.

"From our home, we had a view of the fires ... We could see the clouds becoming darker and darker," said Yoan Urien, who left late on Thursday after police told everyone in his neighbourhood in the town of Biscarrosse to leave. "I was able to find ‌somewhere to take shelter with my pets, but ... it's quite a shock," the 26-year-old told Reuters.

open image in gallery Holidaymakers from Lege-Cap-Ferret disembark from a boat upon their arrival in Arcachon during an evacuation operation of the entire Cap-Ferret peninsula ( AFP/Getty )

The other major fire, which began in nearby Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, is threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula and is the largest so far this season in France, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez told local television. It has ‌torn through more than 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) of forest and burned 80 homes, completely destroying about 50 ‌of them, he said.

"It breaks my heart. Because it's such a pleasant place to live, seeing it go up in smoke is truly sad," said family caregiver Corinne Paillaube. "It's totally apocalyptic," said Ambre Dubos, from the nearby Landes region.

Mapped: Cap Ferret peninsula

Spain struggles to tackle multiple fires amid a heatwave

In Spain, the government declared a national emergency for wildfires for the first time as the blazes in Madrid and the nearby province of Ávila prompted the evacuation of some 20,000 people from towns.

The national emergency means that the nation’s interior ministry, which controls police and security forces, has taken charge of overseeing the firefighting efforts that are being fanned by a heat wave. Temperatures are expected to top 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit) in parts of Spain.

The two major fires west of Madrid merged into one single blaze that had quickly charred 30 square kilometers (11.5 square miles) by Friday afternoon. Regional president Isabel Díaz-Ayuso called it the worst in Madrid's history.

The regional government of Madrid, which spans a wide area around the city, said that around 18,000 people had been evacuated from different villages and towns west of the capital.

open image in gallery Smoke and flames rise as a wildfire advances near La Adrada, Ávila province, Spain. ( AP )

Meanwhile, a blaze in Ávila, less than two hours northwest of Madrid, had consumed 90 square kilometers (34 square miles), causing another 1,500 people to flee.

“In my 60 years I have never seen something like this in my village, I have never seen fire of these dimensions,” Francisco Martínez, the mayor of Burgohondo, whose residents were preventively evacuated in Ávila, told Spain’s national broadcaster TVE.

Spanish television showed video taken by retreating residents of walls of flames topped by long plumes of smoke advancing through woods and scrublands. High winds and hilly terrain complicated efforts by firefighters, who combated the blazes with firetrucks and bulldozers.

“All around the town was smoke and fire, I was scared. Everything was fire and smoke, people were nervous,” 33-year-old Joaquin Espinosa told The Associated Press before he and his neighbors were evacuated fromF the village of Chapinería, located less than an hour's drive west of Madrid.

Strong winds complicate efforts

In one week, Spain has had the worst fires on record for both the regions of Castilla La Mancha and Madrid.

Firefighters were still trying to extinguish Spain’s second-largest ever fire in the Guadalajara province of Castilla La Mancha after it had destroyed some 320 square kilometers (120 square miles) over the last week. Thirteen people were also killed in a fire in southern Spain earlier this month, the deadliest fire in recent memory for Spain.

Spanish Minister for the Ecological Transition Sara Aagesen said that Spain has seen 1,140 square kilometers (440 square miles) already burned this year, more than five times the burned terrain it had through the first half of 2025.

open image in gallery Smoke and flames rise as a wildfire advances near San Martin de Valdeiglesias, Ávila province, Spain. ( AP )

Grande-Marlaska said that in addition to the major fires in Madrid and in Ávila that have required the national government to get directly involved, there are nine serious fires in other parts of Spain.

“The day has been complicated by winds that reach 50 kph (31 mph) and high temperatures,” Grande-Marlaska said.

Sánchez called on Wednesday for a pact between political parties to fight climate change that he said is key to adapting to a more fire-prone climate. Spain has experienced record temperatures in recent summers and forest fires of increasing violence.

Sicily is burning

In Italy, wildfires continued to ravage parts of Sicily, with the central-western province of Agrigento particularly hard hit.

open image in gallery A Canadair drops water over a burning area as a wildfire flares in Sagana in the territory of Monreale, Sicily ( AFP/Getty )

Fueled by temperatures that have topped 40C (104F), low humidity and winds, the blazes have forced scattered evacuations and were blamed for the death of a firefighter responding to a fire in Caltanissetta.

Globally, 2025 was the third-hottest year on record, bringing severe heat waves across Europe. Scientists warn that climate change is exacerbating the frequency and intensity of heat and dryness especially in southeastern Europe, making the region more vulnerable to health impacts and wildfires.

Tyson Fury fulfilled his side of the bargain for a potential heavyweight blockbuster against Anthony Joshua by stopping veteran Polish fighter Mariusz Wach in Pattaya, Thailand.

Around 1,500 fans watched the bout, which had no live broadcast, and saw Fury largely dominate his overmatched 46-year-old opponent, who slipped to his eighth defeat in his last 11 contests.

While Wach remained upright, he was pulled out after the end of the seventh round by his corner, battered into submission by Fury, who made it back-to-back wins in 2026 after a 16-month lay-off.

All eyes will now turn to Joshua’s fight against unheralded Albanian knockout artist Kristian Prenga in Jeddah, Saudi Arabia on Saturday night – although Fury said he is not planning to be in attendance.

If Joshua has his hand raised then it should pave the way for a long-awaited and much-anticipated ‘Battle of Britain’ against fellow former two-time world heavyweight champion Fury.

After Joshua announced he would return to the ring against Prenga – his first fight since being involved in a car crash in December in Nigeria that killed two of his closest friends – Fury also decided on a tune-up, having outpointed Russia’s Arslanbek Makhmudov in April.

For only the fourth time in 39 fights and the first in 15 years, Fury was leaner than his opponent after clocking 265lbs, nearly two stone lighter than Wach, who scaled 291.4lbs at Thursday’s weigh-in.

The 6ft 9in Fury though had the height and reach advantages and used the jab to control the range, as well as switching between orthodox and southpaw stances to confuse his rival.

While Wach is a former world title challenger, losing to Wladimir Klitschko in 2012, he is regarded as a faded force and was stopped inside two rounds by rising British prospect Moses Itauma two years ago.

Wach found the target with the odd right hand but Fury was the busier and more punishing fighter, at one point landing five uppercuts in a row to the cheers of a partisan crowd.

Fury, who has based his training camps in Thailand since reversing his retirement at the start of the year, beat Makhmudov in front of 60,000 fans at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium but was undeterred by fighting in front of a smaller crowd.

Following the end of the seventh round, the contest was waved off by the referee after Wach’s corner indicated their charge was unable to continue as Fury (now 36-2-1, 25KOs) improved his record.

Isabella Williams was one of hundreds of incoming college freshmen left disappointed after Howard University rescinded her admission just days before she was due to move onto campus.

Williams, who was accepted into 42 colleges before accepting an offer to the historically Black private university located in Washington D.C., tearfully shared the disappointing news in a recent Instagram video.

Describing the university as her “dream school,” Williams said: “Never in my life have I been so disappointed. Never in my life have I gotten so far and worked so hard for it to be stripped from me on a random Wednesday.”

In the now-viral post’s caption, she wrote: “I’m supposed to move in on SATURDAY. Howard University has unenrolled 100s of students. Financial aid TOLD ME that my external scholarships would suffice. Please, hold them accountable.”

Speaking to local ABC affiliate WJLA about the debacle, Williams explained that she was disenrolled due to an outstanding balance.

open image in gallery Howard University is a private, historically black institution located in Washington D.C. ( AFP via Getty Images )

open image in gallery Howard University notified more than 500 incoming freshmen of their disenrollment ( Getty )

“They stated that there was no way for us to come back, and that they suggested that we come back for another semester as a transfer student,” she said. “And they gave a little bit of information about how to get scholarship reimbursement in the near future. Now, this was confusing for a multitude of reasons.”

Williams noted that she had received two scholarships from Howard University. “I had an $11,000 scholarship and a $16,000 scholarship that was directly from them,” she said. “And then I had originally it was $13,000 that I had to pay off, but it was actually $12,000 because they let you waive your health insurance.”

She added that she provided document proof to the university that she would pay the remaining balance by August, and was told “everything was fine” and that her “scholarships could come through later.”

The University confirmed to WJLA that it had sent the disenrollment notice to more than 500 “first-time-in-college students whose accounts did not reflect the required enrollment and financial obligations by the previously communicated deadlines.”

“Howard University provided multiple detailed communications throughout March, April, May, June, and July to first-time-in-college students and families on steps needed to secure enrollment for the fall 2026 semester,” the school said in an earlier statement.

open image in gallery Isabella Williams was one of hundreds of incoming Howard University freshmen who were stripped of their admission days before moving on campus ( educated.barbie/Instagram )

The Independent has contacted Howard University for further comment.

Williams’s enrollment has since been restored following her public plea. She remains hopeful that the University will do the same for the other students.

“I’m more so disappointed in the way that Howard is acting, but I’m not disappointed in the school or the promise itself,” she said to the outlet.

In a statement posted Thursday on X, Howard University addressed the “concerns and challenges that students that students and families are experiencing related to the recent enrollment update.”

“The University is reviewing information related to enrollment status, anticipated scholarship funding, and other financial aid, where appropriate,” it continued, “and will consider relevant circumstances regarding pending scholarship awards and financial aid resources for impacted students.”

Sarah Ferguson’s charity, Sarah’s Trust, has formally closed down after the former Duchess of York was embroiled in the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

Days after new revelations emerged about the former duchess’s friendship with the paedophile financier, Sarah Ferguson’s charity announced it would close “for the foreseeable future”.

In a statement made in February, Sarah’s Trust said Ms Ferguson and the board of trustees had agreed “with regret” that the charity would close.

“This has been under discussion and in train for some months,” the statement continued. “We remain extremely proud of the work of the trust over recent years.”

Now, months later, Sarah’s Trust is marked as "removed" on the public register of charities.

The charity, launched in 2020 during the Covid pandemic, provided aid for NHS, care home and hospice staff. It had also secured money to send computers to Ukrainian refugees in Poland.

In February, Sarah’s Trust said Ms Ferguson and the board of trustees had agreed “with regret” that the charity would close (Jordan Pettitt/PA) ( PA Wire )

The Independent has contacted Ferguson’s representatives for comment on the closure of her charity.

The announcement that the charity would close came just days after more than three million documents were published by the US Department of Justice, which revealed she was in contact with Epstein while he was in prison for soliciting sex from a minor.

Files released by the DoJ suggested that Ms Ferguson visited Epstein with her two daughters, Beatrice and Eugenie, just days after Epstein was released from prison for soliciting prostitution from a minor.

In one email dated 28 July 2009, six days after he left prison, Epstein caught up with his accomplice Ghislaine Maxwell, telling her how many people were billed to visit him that week.

“Ferg and the two girls come yesterday [sic],” he said. “Today [redacted].. tomomwo sultan , yesterday farkas„ sat jarecki, sunday [redacted],, monday novak [sic].”

In other emails, Ms Ferguson said Epstein was the “brother I have always wished for” and later said she needed £20,000 for rent following the collapse of her business venture.

In one email exchange from 2009, the then Duchess of York updated Epstein on potential opportunities for her business brands and books.

“In just one week, after your lunch, it seems the energy has lifted,” she wrote.

“I have never been more touched by a friends [sic] kindness than your compliment to me infront of my girls.

“Thank you Jeffrey for being the brother I have always wished for.”

Being named in the documents does not indicate wrongdoing.

Ms Ferguson lost her duchess title when her ex-husband Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, relinquished his Duke of York title over his links with Epstein.

News.title: Woman charged in connection with ‘dissident republican bomb’ seized near Irish border
News.content:

Read our Privacy notice

A woman has been charged after police intercepted a car comb near the Irish border on Friday.

Gardaí investigating the incident, which involved a suspected dissident republican bomb, have charged a woman in her 20s in connection with the case.

The accused, who was the driver of the car, is due to appear before a special sitting of Trim District Court in Co Meath on Friday evening.

In an intelligence-led swoop, members of the Garda’s Special Detective Unit stopped the vehicle travelling on the N2 south of Carrickmacross, Co Monaghan on Wednesday afternoon.

The Garda described the bomb seized from the vehicle as “extremely significant”.

It is understood the device found contained suspected military-grade explosives.

Garda sources have described the bomb as “highly sophisticated” and “advanced”.

Another suspect, a man aged in his 40s, remains in custody at a Garda station in the Dublin area.

Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly confirmed details of the operation as he spoke to media at a Garda graduation event in Co Tipperary on Friday morning.

open image in gallery Ireland’s Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan described the seizure as “very worrying” ( PA )

“To be clear, what we found was an extremely significant seizure,” he said.

“So this was an explosive device.”

Commissioner Kelly added: “Any seizure of this nature is really concerning.

“However, we certainly know that there are a small minority of dissident republicans who did not agree with the Good Friday Agreement. They did not put weapons and explosives (out of use), they didn’t, you know, go through with the proper process in relation to decommissioning.

“So that is something that we continue to deal with.

“There’s a small minority of these individuals – I would describe them as radicalised republicans – and this is a threat that we’re going to continue to face for some time in An Garda Síochána.”

Ireland’s Minister for Justice Jim O’Callaghan described the seizure as “very worrying”.

“I think it evidences the fact that there is an ongoing threat in respect of dissident republican activity,” he said.

“But I also know that there’s been great co-operation between the PSNI and An Garda Síochána and, I think, I suppose the developments recently and the work of An Garda Síochána indicate the benefits of having that close co-operation between the PSNI and An Garda Síochána.”

PSNI Assistant Chief Constable Davy Beck said police on both sides of the Irish border shared a “joint commitment” to tackle the dissident republican terror threat.

open image in gallery DUP leader Gavin Robinson described the development as “chilling”. ( Rebecca Black/PA )

“I very much welcome this significant seizure and the arrests made by our colleagues in An Garda Síochána, with whom we work very closely on a daily basis,” he said.

Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant commended the Garda for thwarting a potential attack.

“Intercepting a dangerous device like this undoubtedly saved lives and kept communities safe on both sides of the border,” he said.

“Strong cross-border security co-operation remains as vital as ever.”

DUP leader Gavin Robinson described the development as “chilling”.

The east Belfast MP questioned whether the Irish government needed to increase its focus on tackling dissident republicanism.

“All those involved in stopping this deserve enormous credit,” he said.

“Their actions may have prevented innocent families from suffering unimaginable tragedy.”

Sinn Féin Stormont Assembly member Gerry Kelly described those responsible for the explosive device as “reckless”.

“Those responsible represent no one, are void of support and have nothing positive to offer our communities. Their actions are entirely reckless,” he said.

“Those involved should abandon their futile actions, leave the stage once and for all, and allow our communities to continue moving forward together in peace.”
