World.title: Epstein scandal reaches Hungary again after unexpected death of agent who hunted out Hungarian girls
World.content:
The Epstein scandal has reached Hungary once more with the sudden death of a model scout who allegedly searched for girls in the country, as the ripples of the affair continue to shake even the old British royal establishment. Daniel Siad, 69, was under investigation in France by prosecutors specialising in human trafficking, on suspicion of rape and other offences, but had not yet been questioned. His body was found at home, and investigators have ordered an autopsy.

Very close to each other

Siad’s name appears more than a thousand times in the US Department of Justice Epstein files released this year. The documents suggest that the model scout worked closely with Jeffrey Epstein for years, regularly finding women from the fashion industry for him while the billionaire covered his travel costs on several occasions through bank transfers.

According to the files, Siad travelled through villages in Eastern Europe, but also went to Cuba and Sweden in search of models. In a 2014 email, he compared his work to fishing, saying patience was needed because “sometimes you catch fish quickly, sometimes nothing” — in rather poor English, as The Guardian noted. On the basis of the Epstein files, he remained in contact with the billionaire until 2016.

Photo: his photo uploaded to the registry of sexual offenders. Source: Wikimedia Commons.

Hungary in the files

The released documents do not only shed light on Siad’s activities; they also contain several Hungary-related references. In one 2009 email, Siad asked the billionaire for money so he could spend the following months in Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Poland and Hungary, where, in his own words, he wanted to look for girls in “small villages”. He ended the message by saying he would have “a big surprise” when Epstein arrived in Paris, though it was never made clear what he meant.

The correspondence also shows that in 2015 Epstein asked Siad in an email what had happened to “the Hungarian girl”. Several other emails refer to Hungarian girls, as well as to a Hungarian woman who sent Epstein photographs and videos, then wrote that she had cut ties with “Daniel’s friend” because he had treated her badly.

Budapest keeps appearing

Budapest also crops up repeatedly in the millions of Epstein documents released in January. The papers show Epstein corresponding with the Norwegian film producer Haakon Gundersen, who has Hungarian links, about the transfer and sale of a flat at 70 Király Street in Budapest, Telex reported at the time. The emails also suggest that Epstein repeatedly indicated he was heading to Budapest, or was already in the city.

Short messages in the files include:

“I’ll send someone to Budapest.”

“I’ll be in Budapest.”

“I’m in Budapest. On my way to you.”

“I’m in Budapest. Which flat?”

The documents do not, however, show exactly when those trips took place. After Telex published its report, Gundersen’s production company issued a statement denying that he had any business or other relationship with the American billionaire. The statement said Epstein had never been to any property or business connected to Gundersen.

Hungarian names and models

The files also mention the literary agent John Brockman recommending network scientist Albert-László Barabási to Epstein in 2012. Epstein wanted to meet him and contacted him by email in 2014, but the planned meeting never happened. After the documents were made public, Barabási said he had not known the correspondence would be released, that he had never met him, and that there was no further contact beyond the brief email exchange in 2014.

Another document says Epstein sent a package to economist János Kornai in 2005, though the files do not reveal what it contained.

Owner of Budapest property linked to Epstein files says he was threatened

The documents also name two Hungarian top models. In a 2013 email exchange, businessman Tancredi Marchiolo asked Epstein whether he knew Barbara Palvin, and the billionaire replied that he did not. Enikő Mihalik’s name appears in a 2017 message, when he asked an acquaintance whether he had seen attractive women at a New York gym; Mihalik was mentioned in the reply, along with a note about the models present.

Cause of death under review

Daniel Siad had previously denied all allegations against him. He said he had only introduced women to Epstein through legitimate model castings and did not know the billionaire was committing crimes. According to Siad, he had not supplied either minors or adults who became victims of sexual offences. He also told French television that Epstein had abused his trust and that he was not in a position to recognise the danger.

After his death, French authorities opened an inquiry to determine the cause, and an autopsy has been ordered.

Epstein himself has been dead since 2019, after hanging himself in his cell following a second arrest on serious charges.

Hungarian names emerge in Epstein files: models, recruiters and Eastern Europe

World.title: Romanian director Alina Șerban’s debut film “I Matter” to premiere at Venice Film Festival
World.content:
“I Matter” (“Eu contez”), the feature film debut of Romanian director Alina Șerban (in photo), will have its world premiere at the 83rd edition of the Venice International Film Festival, taking place from September 1-12.

Written and directed by Alina Șerban, one of the few Roma female directors in the world, “I Matter” is a co-production between Romania (microFILM), Germany (2Pilots Filmproduction), and Belgium (Frakas Productions, Lemming Film), exploring themes such as overcoming fear, hope, and self-acceptance, according to the press release.

Spoken in Romanian and Romani, the film tells the story of Rebeca, a young Roma woman who is about to leave the foster care center where she grew up.

“We very rarely see Roma characters who live complex human experiences beyond stereotypes. And stories about what it means to be a girl, Roma, and part of the child protection system are almost nonexistent. Through ‘I Matter’ I wanted to build a bridge toward a deeper understanding of these experiences and, above all, to tell a story about humanity. The fact that this film is beginning its journey in Venice means a great deal to me,” said Alina Șerban.

The film was developed over more than four years together with young people from the social protection system. During this period, Alina Șerban created several documentary short films and theater performances alongside them.

The film’s cast includes Denisa Farcaș, Sorin Mihai, Angelina Pavel, Vanessa Dancea, Raisa Mihai, Juno (Alexandru Stancu), Alina Berzunțeanu, and Natalia Călin. Alongside them, 16 children and young people residing in the Casa Iosif and Casa Sara foster centers, part of the Măgurele Christian Social Ensemble in Bucharest, also appear in the film.

The Venice International Film Festival / Mostra Internazionale d'Arte Cinematografica will take place from September 2-12, 2026. “I Matter” has been selected alongside seven other titles in the Spotlight section, dedicated to audience films characterized by innovation and creativity in the way they engage with viewers. The film is competing for the Audience Award offered by Armani Beauty and the Luigi de Laurentiis Award for Best Debut, awarded by an international jury.

Winner of the Best Actress award at the German Actors’ Association Awards for her role in Gipsy Queen (2019), Alina Șerban is a graduate of the prestigious Tisch School of the Arts (New York), Royal Academy of Dramatic Art – RADA (London), and UNATC. In 2024, she was decorated by the president of Romania with the Order of Cultural Merit, in the rank of Knight.

She is the first Roma film and theater director in Romania and, for more than a decade, has developed artistic projects dedicated to children and young people from disadvantaged backgrounds, as well as Roma communities.

World.title: Anti-corruption prosecutors detain three directors of state-owned Romanian defense companies
World.content:
Romania’s National Anticorruption Directorate (DNA) officially announced on Friday, July 24, that it has detained three directors from companies within Romania's defense industry, all accused of taking bribes.

The three are Mihai Rafiu (general manager of Uzina Mecanică București), Tiberiu Alexandru Pîrvu (general manager of Uzina Mecanică Plopeni), and Liliana Sorescu (commercial director of Uzina Mecanică Plopeni).

Alongside the three, an administrator of several commercial companies was also detained, accused of giving bribes and complicity in giving bribes.

During searches, prosecutors found EUR 500,000 in cash at the home of Tiberiu Pârvu Alexandru. Authorities say Rafiu, for his part, allegedly received RON 48,000 from the businessman detained in this case, divided into 12 installments, according to the official DNA statement.

Tiberiu Pârvu Alexandru also allegedly received RON 25,900 from the same businessman "related to contracts concluded with the commercial companies effectively managed by defendant V.M."

The same businessman allegedly also bribed Liliana Sorescu. According to DNA, the total amount she allegedly received as bribes was RON 24,250, in several installments.

In addition, DNA also claimed that another businessman, who owns a company with contracts with Uzina Mecanică Plopeni, allegedly gave Liliana Sorescu USD 3,800, for "placing orders and carrying out the formalities necessary for the acceptance of the goods delivered by the respective companies."

Liliana Sorescu allegedly claimed that the dollars she received were counterfeit and requested the same amount once again, which she allegedly received in lei. "The contracts concluded by the two factories with the aforementioned commercial companies mainly concerned maintenance services, the purchase of materials, and the provision of services," DNA emphasized.

Reacting to the detention of the three directors, economy minister Irineu Darau said that "in general, the defense industry is an extremely sensitive subject. I am convinced that for some it is also a subject of temptation. A strong Romanian state must identify anyone connected to the defense industry who engages in dishonest activities.”

ROMARM, Romania's national state-owned defense company and the country's primary producer and exporter of military equipment, said in connection with the detention that it will support any legal action aimed at strengthening and reviving the defense industry.

The company noted that the problems within its subsidiaries have been known for some time and have been repeatedly brought to the attention of the Ministry of Economy, without answer.

The company's general manager, Răzvan Pîrcălăbescu, said in a statement cited by Digi24 that the reform plan was drafted by ROMARM's management, discussed with institutional partners, approved by the Board of Directors, and submitted to the Ministry of Economy for final approval, but so far the institution has made no decision.

World.title: Asia-born home improvement chain MR.DIY opens location at Bucharest’s Colosseum Mall
World.content:
MR.DIY, one of the world’s leading home improvement and lifestyle retailers, announced the opening of a location at Bucharest’s Colosseum Mall on Thursday, July 23.

Spanning over 800 sqm and developed following an investment of nearly half a million euros, the new MR.DIY store represents one of the most important openings within the retailer’s current national expansion plan, according to the press release.

The store offers a comprehensive one-stop-shop format offering customers access to thousands of practical everyday products across categories such as home improvement, household items, home organization, hardware and tools, stationery, toys, decorations, electrical accessories, car accessories and lifestyle products.

The opening is part of a process of diversification ongoing at the mall. Earlier this spring, Colosseum Mall also welcomed dm dogerie markt and Planeta Arthur bookstore.

The new store has been designed to deliver an accessible and efficient shopping experience, allowing customers to discover a broad assortment of products for everyday needs under one roof.

“This new store reflects our commitment to bringing the MR.DIY concept closer to Romanian consumers through accessible locations, a broad product assortment and affordable prices. Romania is an important market in MR.DIY’s European expansion strategy, and each new opening represents another step in building a strong long-term presence locally,” said Cătălin Secăreanu, representative of MR.DIY in Romania.

Established in Malaysia in 2005 with a single hardware store in Kuala Lumpur, MR.DIY has grown into one of Asia’s leading home improvement and lifestyle retailers, with a continuously expanding international presence across multiple markets. Today, MR.DIY operates in 15 countries worldwide, with more than 5,700 stores across Asia, Europe and other international markets.

World.title: EUR 80 million refinancing for Bucharest underground telecommunications network operator Netcity
World.content:
Meridiam and its partners have successfully closed the EUR 80 million refinancing of Netcity Telecom, the operator of Bucharest's underground telecommunications network, the company announced.

According to the company, the refinancing operation, led end-to-end by Meridiam, represents the first project finance bond issuance in the country, and establishes a new market record with tenors of up to 26.5 years, surpassing Meridiam's previous 18-year market benchmark achieved in 2022.

The operation also provides flexibility to support a future expansion of the Netcity Telecom network and new digital infrastructure developments across Bucharest, Meridiam said.

Netcity Telecom has been operating the underground telecommunications network in Bucharest since 2008, in a 49-year concession agreement with the Bucharest City Hall.

It has so far developed more than 3,000 kilometers of underground telecommunications infrastructure across Bucharest, while removing overhead cables. Today, the network serves around 70,000 buildings, representing approximately half of all buildings in the city, and provides internet access to nearly 600,000 homes and office premises.

Netcity Telecom has worked with several districts of Bucharest in designing and deploying dedicated fiber networks for municipal CCTV projects. The company has also contributed to the implementation of the pilot phase of the new Bucharest Traffic Management System, and is currently involved in Smart School initiatives.

Meridiam has an 80% stake in Netcity Telecom, alongside E-INFRA Group (20%), a Romanian group active in the energy, construction, and telecommunications sectors.

Meridiam, an independent investment Benefit Corporation and asset manager, was founded in 2005 by Thierry Déau. The firm specializes in the development, financing, and long-term management of public infrastructure across three sectors: sustainable mobility, critical public services, and innovative low-carbon solutions. With offices in Addis Ababa, Amman, Dakar, Istanbul, Johannesburg, Libreville, Luxembourg, Paris, Vienna, and Washington, Meridiam manages USD24 billion and more than 130 projects to date.

World.title: Romanian manufacturer TeraPlast inaugurates polyethylene pipe factory in Spain
World.content:
Romanian building materials manufacturer TeraPlast Group inaugurated its TeraPlast Iberia polyethylene pipe factory in Spain, strengthening its expansion into Western European markets. The facility, located near Bilbao, is expected to serve customers across Spain, France, and North Africa.

The factory, inaugurated on July 23, is located in Okondo, in Spain's Álava province, about 20 kilometers from Bilbao. It has an annual production capacity of 16,000 tonnes and employs 79 people.

The opening follows TeraPlast's acquisition of the facility and forms part of the group's international expansion strategy after earlier investments in the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria, and Croatia.

“Romanian industry can compete and thrive at European level, and we demonstrate it through actions, not idealistic speeches. Following our expansion into the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria and Croatia, our entry into the Spanish market marks another important step in our international growth strategy,” said Dorel Goia, chairman of the TeraPlast Board of Directors.

The company plans to invest EUR 4 million in the Spanish factory over the next three years to increase production by 60% and achieve an EBITDA margin of more than 10%.

“The expanded production capacity will serve the markets of Spain, France, and North Africa. This will enable us to reduce leverage while generating returns on our investment for the benefit of the group's shareholders," Goia added.

According to the company, the factory has an established customer base in Spain, France, and Germany and will serve as a regional hub for the group's operations in Western Europe.

TeraPlast Group is the largest polymer processor in Southeastern Europe and operates production facilities in Romania, the Republic of Moldova, Hungary, Austria, Croatia, and Spain. Its parent company, TeraPlast SA, is listed on the Bucharest Stock Exchange under the symbol TRP.

World.title: Otokar starts deliveries of Romanian-built Cobra II armored vehicles
World.content:
Turkish defense manufacturer Otokar has begun delivering Cobra II tactical armored vehicles manufactured locally to the Romanian Armed Forces, marking the start of serial production at its plant in Mediaș. More than 780 of the 1,059 vehicles ordered by Romania are scheduled to be built at the local facility over the next five years.

The company said the first Cobra II vehicles manufactured entirely in Mediaș left the factory this week. A total of 216 vehicles, including four different variants, are scheduled for delivery in 2026.

The vehicles are being produced at Automecanica Mediaș, which has become Otokar's first manufacturing facility in the European Union. According to the company, the factory carries out the entire production process rather than only final assembly, giving Romania the capability to manufacture 4x4 armored vehicles locally.

“Romanian-made Cobra II deliveries have just begun. The first Cobra II vehicles manufactured entirely in Mediaș left the factory gates yesterday heading to the Romanian Armed Forces,” said Yusuf Fettahlıoğlu, General Manager of Automecanica Mediaş.

The Mediaș plant covers around 140,000 square meters and has been equipped to manufacture the vehicles to the same production standards as Otokar's facilities in Türkiye.

“Beyond the production line, the investment brings Romania what matters over the long term: advanced production know-how, technology transfer and engineering capabilities. The Mediaș plant is becoming a regional land-systems hub, capable of supporting not only production for the Romanian armed forces but also future export opportunities linked to NATO and European Union defence programmes,” stated Yusuf Fettahlıoğlu.

The Cobra II is a modular 4x4 tactical armored vehicle introduced in 2013 and currently used by more than 20 military and security organizations across 13 countries, including NATO members. For Romania, Otokar is producing several variants, including personnel carrier, reconnaissance, remote weapon station, CBRN reconnaissance, and ambulance versions.

The project has also expanded employment at the Mediaș facility, where the workforce now exceeds 300 people and is expected to grow to nearly 400 as production ramps up.

World.title: Romania wins one gold, seven silver medals at first Central European Olympiad in AI
World.content:
The Romanian delegation to the first Central European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (CEOAI), held in Cluj-Napoca between July 14-19, won one gold medal and seven silver medals, according to the Ministry of Education.

The event represented a historic moment for the international AI community, bringing together more than 90 contestants from over 20 European countries, along with invited delegations from around the world.

During the competition, contestant had to design, train, and optimize their own artificial intelligence models, starting from completely new datasets and requirements. In the two competition days, students tackled problems in diverse fields, such as artificial intelligence model interpretability, optical character recognition (OCR), mathematical and physical modeling, computer vision, and the security of machine learning models through steganography techniques. The competition tested not only the participants' technical knowledge but also their creativity, analytical ability, and rapid adaptation to problems without standard solutions, according to G4Media.

Following the interest shown by high school students from across Europe, the competition, initially known as the Central European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (CEOAI), received a new name, becoming the European Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (EUROAI).

Emil-Andrei Burloi, a student at the International Computer Science High School of Bucharest, ranked third in the overall competition standings, winning Romania's first gold medal in international AI competitions in 2026. Subsequently, following the decision of the Ministry of Education and Research for the Romanian delegation to participate as a guest delegation, the official ranking was adjusted in accordance with the competition regulations.

Silver medals went to Ciortea-Suciu Andrei from the "Silvania" National College, Zalău, Morariu Tudor from the International Computer Science High School of Bucharest, Ilie-Goga Radu from the "Tudor Vianu" National College of Computer Science Bucharest, Dobre Darius-Adrian from the "Matei Basarab" National College of Computer Science in Râmnicu Vâlcea, Apostol Mihnea-Petru from the same highschool, Nistor Iulian from the “Tiberiu Popoviciu" Computer Science High School in Cluj-Napoca, and Asandei Ștefan-Alexandru from the Iași National College.

The national team was coordinated by Miron Radu (Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași) and Ciprian Păduraru (University of Bucharest). The national team's qualification was achieved following the ROAI stages, organized in partnership with Genesis College and the "Tudor Vianu" National College of Computer Science, with the support of the Nitro Association, Babeș-Bolyai University, the University of Bucharest, and Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași.

Throughout the selection stages, hundreds of students from across the country solved original machine learning and deep learning problems, training their own models and demonstrating advanced skills in a field at the intersection of computer science, mathematics, and research.

World.title: Romania to receive EUR 2.15 bln in NATO funding for fuel pipeline network expansion
World.content:
President Nicușor Dan announced on Thursday, July 23, that following more than five years of negotiations, NATO approved the eastward expansion of its fuel pipeline network, a strategic result for Romania.

The Alliance will fund the expansion with EUR 27 billion over the next 20 years, of which Romania will receive EUR 2.15 billion. The new network will also cross Romanian territory, will have both military and civilian uses, and will create important opportunities for the Romanian economy and companies.

"Romania achieves an important strategic result within NATO. After more than five years of negotiations, the Alliance has approved the eastward expansion of NATO’s fuel pipeline network, an essential project for strengthening security and military mobility on the Eastern Flank. The decision also comes as a result of lessons learned after Russia invaded Ukraine, which demonstrated how important logistical infrastructure is for collective defense,” the president said on Facebook.

Romania has been actively involved from the very beginning in the negotiation, through the efforts of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of National Defence, and Romania’s Delegation to NATO, according to the head of state.

“This project strengthens Romania’s role as a frontline allied state on the Black Sea and enhances our country’s strategic connectivity with NATO allies,” Dan said.

Specifically, the NATO Fuel Supply Chain Capability Program will modernize NATO’s existing fuel storage and distribution infrastructure. “It will support new facilities, including pipelines, in the eastern and south-eastern part of the Alliance and ensure NATO forces have the energy supplies they need for warfighting readiness,” according to the NATO press release.

The investment is part of NATO’s 2027–2031 Common Funding Resource Plan, which sets out how the Alliance will invest in shared priorities over the next five years. As part of the decision, Allies agreed the 2027 funding ceilings for NATO’s Military Budget, Civil Budget and Security Investment Programme, raising total common funding to up to EUR 6.5 billion.

The plan also provides resources for priority support to Ukraine, including the NATO Security Assistance and Training to Ukraine initiative and the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre.

World.title: Serbian Flag on Cocaine Haul from Ecuador is a Clue – Not Proof
World.content:
On July 21, the Italian authorities seized 650 packages with more than 770 kilograms of cocaine at the port of Vado Ligure. The drugs were hidden among pallets of bananas in a refrigerated container from Ecuador.

Concealing cocaine in commercial shipments of fresh fruit, particularly bananas from Ecuador, is a well-known method used by criminal actors, including groups from the Balkans.

The Vado Ligure seizure, therefore, fits a broader pattern of maritime cocaine trafficking into Europe.

In Serbia, however, it wasn’t the size of the seizure or its route that attracted most attention but the Serbian flag displayed on some of the packages.

Although the comments posted under the media reports offer only a snapshot of public opinion, they reveal two recurring reactions.

World.title: Law and Justice Suffers Split Ahead of Poland’s 2027 Election
World.content:
Following a months-long power struggle, more than 30 MPs – including former prime minister Mateusz Morawiecki – are set to be expelled from the Law and Justice party, in the biggest rupture seen on the Polish right in many years.

Law and Justice, or PiS, is Poland’s largest opposition party and one of the country’s two dominant political forces, alongside the governing Civic Coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. The split could sharply reduce PiS’s chances of returning to power in next year’s parliamentary election.

On early Friday afternoon, PiS leader Jaroslaw Kaczynski announced that “around 30-something” of the party’s 186 MPs had effectively chosen to leave after refusing to sign declarations of loyalty. The documents required them to state that they did not belong to any political associations operating within the party – an obvious reference to Development Plus (Rozwoj Plus), an organisation created by Morawiecki, until now one of PiS’s deputy leaders.

“Everyone knew what they were supposed to sign, and knew the consequences of not signing,” Kaczynski said. “And so they made the decision they did.”

Kaczynski has been PiS’s undisputed leader and chief power broker for more than two decades, selecting loyal candidates for prime minister who largely continued to defer to him once in office. Morawiecki was initially one of them, serving as prime minister between 2017 and 2023.

But in recent years, Morawiecki – an economist, former banker and comparatively moderate conservative – has grown increasingly impatient with Kaczynski’s dominance. He has pushed for changes to both the party’s internal structure and its political program, arguing that PiS was failing to speak convincingly to younger voters and entrepreneurs.

Friday’s rupture was the culmination of months of increasingly open conflict.

“Until the very last moment, we fought for the unity of the Law and Justice camp,” Morawiecki said at a press conference. “We could not accept being forced to sign a loyalty pledge.”

He accused the party leadership of using ultimatums and political blackmail to discard a strategy that had been agreed only recently.

Morawiecki did not formally announce the creation of a new party. He did, however, declare the beginning of “a new chapter in Poland’s political history”, promise a major nationwide tour and announce that his camp would soon present a new political program.

He said his political circle now included 40 MPs (which stands at odds with Kaczynski’s estimate), one senator and three members of the European Parliament, describing it as a “very strong representation”. Its offer, he said, would reach beyond PiS’s traditional base and target young people, entrepreneurs, local-government officials and even some voters currently supporting the governing coalition.

Morawiecki presented his project as a modern, patriotic and pro-state conservative force, capable of responding to social and economic change without falling back on outdated ideas.

The electoral consequences could be enormous. An Opinia24 poll conducted before the split tested precisely such a scenario. With PiS united, the party would receive 23 per cent of the vote, behind Civic Coalition on 31.6 per cent. When respondents were offered a separate Morawiecki-led Rozwoj Plus list, support for PiS fell to 17.7 per cent, while Morawiecki’s group received 6.2 per cent. Civic Coalition remained clearly ahead on 30.9 per cent.

Tusk responded with a single cutting line: “They are fighting so hard for party unity that there won’t be one stone left standing.”

Deputy Prime Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski was blunter: “Kaczynski went all in and lost.”

World.title: Week in Review: A Fighting Spirit
World.content:
Turkey’s opposition political scene is heating up. On July 21, Ozgur Ozel announced that he was leaving the main opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, to establish a new party.

The news followed a crisis triggered two months ago, when a court annulled Ozel’s election as CHP leader at an earlier party congress, restoring his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu, as leader. Ozel’s new party looks set to take a majority of the CHP’s MPs and voters. But can it be turned into a political force capable of taking on the ruling party?

World.title: Turkey Gets New Main Opposition Party Following Opposition Split
World.content:
Opposition leader, Ozgur Ozel, waves to crowds during a rally in Izmir, Turkey, 26 May 2026. Photo: EPA/STRINGER

Former party chairman Ozgur Ozel announced on Friday that he and 90 lawmakers had resigned from the Republican People’s Party, CHP, to establish the New Party.

Ozel’s decision marks the latest stage in a crisis that began on May 21, when a court annulled the CHP congress that had elected him chairman and reinstated his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu.

Ozel said he hoped the New Party would “be beneficial for our country, our nation, our party, and all of us”, as he signed the document for the foundation of his new party.

Meanwhile, 90 other MPs also resigned from the CHP, making the New Party Turkey’s new main opposition party. The CHP lost its main opposition role after 23 years, retaining only 44 MPs.

President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, has the largest number of seats in parliament, with 277.

The court in May cited alleged voting fraud as the reason for reinstating Kilicdaroglu but Ozel and his supporters saw the ruling as blatant judicial interference in the party’s affairs.

Police entered CHP headquarters four days later to enforce the ruling. Kilicdaroglu’s administration subsequently began disciplinary proceedings against figures associated with Ozel and promised political and organisational “purification”.

Ozel and his allies argue that the judicial intervention and subsequent internal purge have eliminated any possibility of the CHP winning the next elections.

Kilicdaroglu has been removing key CHP figures and local party administration since he took office.

“We opened up a new road because they blocked all the others. We are opening up that road now. Are you ready to march to power? We will march to power,” Ozel said on July 21 in parliament.

Ekrem Imamoglu, jailed Mayor of Istanbul and an opposition presidential candidate, is one of Ozel’s main partners. He is behind bars for alleged corruption – charges he describes as politically motivated. Imamoglu supported Ozel at the 2023 CHP congress and led the internal resistance within the party against Kilicdaroglu.

His jailing and the developments around the CHP come as President Erdogan and his government do their utmost to thwart any opposition challenge to their years-long rule.

In addition to the annulment of the party congress, dozens of CHP mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terrorism charges in recent years.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have accused the government of using the judiciary to crush its political rivals in what they describe as an unprecedented crackdown.

Ozel’s new party is generating excitement in opposition ranks – but according to experts translating a buzz into a political force capable of challenging President Erdogan will not be easy.

World.title: Fake Social Media Accounts Target Albania Protest Supporters
World.content:
After weeks of protests demanding his resignation, Prime Minister Edi Rama accused social media algorithms of having “poured gasoline on the fire” of Albania’s so-called Flamingo Revolution.

“The more views you get, the more influence you have. The more influence you have, the more power you hold. Power over whom? Over the slaves of the algorithms – over all of us,” Rama told parliamentarians from his governing Socialist Party.

Days later, he returned to the theme of social media manipulation after visiting the picturesque mountain village of Theth, where last year the government demolished dozens of illegally built holiday chalets, prompting locals to demonstrate.

Rama posted screenshots on Facebook of what he said were more than a dozen fake accounts who had commented on posts criticising his tourism development plans for Albania’s mountain regions.

World.title: Democracy Digest: Russian Hackers Linked to FSB Target Slovakia
World.content:
Hungary’s chief prosecutor resigns; ex-Austrian chancellor Kurz on MCC’s payroll

Hungary’s chief prosecutor, Balint Gabor Nagy, resigned this week amid mounting pressure from the new Tisza-led government. PM Peter Magyar welcomed the decision. Nagy was appointed by the previous government of Viktor Orban in 2025 for a nine-year term and was regarded as one of its key officeholders. Nagy said he was resigning in order to preserve the dignity and independence of the national prosecutor’s office. “The prosecutor’s office must not become an instrument in conflicts between political actors, nor can it become a battlefield for short-term political interests or power struggles,” Nagy argued in his resignation letter. If accepted, his resignation will take effect on August 25. Magyar has demanded the resignation of key officeholders of the Orban administration following his landslide election victory on April 12. He identified the state president, the chief prosecutor, the president of the Supreme Court and the president of the Constitutional Court as among those who needed to step down in order to achieve genuine regime change in Hungary and dismantle the deep state behind the Orban system. Magyar originally demanded their withdrawal by the end of May, but the process is taking somewhat longer. However, this week he achieved three objectives at once via a constitutional amendment passed on July 13: he secured the departure of the president, the chief prosecutor and the president of the Constitutional Court. Removing the president of the Supreme Court in such a manner could raise rule-of-law concerns but, according to the latest constitutional amendment, he can now be voted out of office by the judges themselves. The move clears the way for potential investigations into Orban’s close business associates or even family members, as Nagy can no longer block them.

It emerged this week that Austria’s former conservative chancellor, Sebastian Kurz, was on the payroll of the Mathias Corvinus Collegium (MCC), a Fidesz-aligned think tank and foundation which in 2020 received a huge endowment from the Hungarian state in the form of assets worth 1.3-1.4 billion euros. Kurz confirmed the information to the Austrian weekly Falter, but said that after Orban’s election defeat he immediately returned around 110,000 euros to the institution. After resigning from office, Kurz maintained close ties with Orban and his Fidesz party. Officially, he served as an adviser to assist the MCC’s acquisition of Austria’s private Modul University in Vienna and received 10,000 euros a month for his involvement, although there is no evidence that he carried out any such work. The MCC acquired a 90 per cent stake in Modul in 2023, while the remaining 10 per cent stayed with the Vienna Chamber of Commerce. Hungary’s new government has already announced it will dissolve the MCC and return its assets to the Hungarian state, which could lead to the bizarre situation where the Hungarian state inherits an Austrian university. Frank Furedi, the head of the MCC’s Brussels branch, which also benefited massively from taxpayer money, has announced earlier this month his institution is seeking new financing but insisted that it operates independently so cannot just be closed down by the Hungarian government. It is becoming increasingly clear that Orban was not only an ideological ally of many far-right and Eurosceptic leaders, but also provided a financial lifeline to many when they were out of office. The MCC also offered lucrative fellowships to Western politicians who praised Orban in the international media and at conferences. Kurz was a regular guest at MCC events and the Orban government firmly believed he would eventually return to government in Austria.

World.title: The Biggest Question Is Not Hungary’s Next President but Its Next Constitution
World.content:
Orban’s shameless resistance – against what exactly?

The former prime minister did not take up his parliamentary mandate after the election that his party so resoundingly lost, but he is still president of the Fidesz party. He declared on Wednesday that after the constitutional amendment removing Sulyok, the rule of law has ceased to exist in Hungary; from now on, there is only tyranny.

After 16 years spent consolidating power and appointing loyal officials to every independent institution, Orban now contends that the actions of the new government are illegitimate because it is seeking to monopolise power. Therefore, Fidesz won’t participate in the election of officials in the place of those who were removed, because it considers the new officials also to be illegitimate. Beyond the state president, this will comprise four constitutional judge vacancies, because the constitutional amendment passed by Tisza also reintroduced the 70-year retirement age for constitutional court judges and four older than that will now have to retire on September 1.

Orban recalled that, according to the constitution, everyone has the right to lawfully resist attempts to secure exclusive control of political power. He promised that Fidesz would support anyone engaged in such resistance. At this point it is worth reminding that at the time he was prime minister, those who expressed similar resistance were usually labelled traitors and foreign agents – but “the times they are a-changin’,” as Bob Dylan sang.

It is likely that with its resistance agenda, Fidesz wants to undermine the new government’s constitution-drafting plans. Prime Minister Magyar has made it explicit that in a constitution-making process seen starting in September Hungarian society would be involved, which is in sharp contrast with the exclusively elite-driven constitution-drafting practices that Hungarians have so far experienced.

By calling on its supporters to resist and depicting the new government’s rule as arbitrary, Fidesz probably also hopes to put people off participating in the constitution-drafting process so that it can label any new constitution illegitimate. Yet this could easily backfire, as the current Fundamental Law was practically written by two Fidesz politicians on a tablet, after a postal consultation with citizens full of biased questions and simplified answer options. This level of transparency and social involvement is not that difficult to surpass, even if Fidesz eventually ends up boycotting the process.

Beyond its legitimacy, the key question about any new constitution is whether and how it will be able to prevent a similar concentration of power to what we witnessed over the past 16 years. This might entail various institutional solutions, depending on the outcome of the consultations in the constitution-making process.

It would be worth considering the reintroduction of bicameralism where, if the right institutional balance is found, the upper chamber could function as a counterbalance to the government and its majority in the lower house. Referendums should also be made functional. Though they currently exist on paper, it is practically impossible to hold a legally binding referendum due to the high turnout threshold and the extensive list of prohibited subjects. Most important of all, the electoral rules and the constitutional provisions governing legislation and institutions must guarantee that no single party can amend the constitution or entrench its priorities in cardinal laws, and that no single party can pack independent institutions with loyalists, hollowing them out from within.

Finding the right constitutional solutions to all these matters is far more important than which person will hold the presidency for an interim period of one or two years.

Bea Bakó is an independent researcher, she holds a PhD in constitutional law and co-authors the Hungarian newsletter Gemišt.

The opinions expressed are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of BIRN.

World.title: Drone Down: Someone’s Messing with Satnav Signals over Protest-Hit Serbia
World.content:
GNSS comprises four major networks: US Global Positioning System, or GPS, the European Union’s Galileo, Russia’s GLONASS, and China’s BeiDou.

They form a critical part of modern infrastructure. Besides guiding aircrafts, ships and vehicles, such systems are used in the energy sector, telecommunications, geodesy, maritime navigation, precision agriculture and numerous industrial systems that depend on accurate positioning and timing.

“It is used by almost every sector of industry,” said a radio frequency and telecommunications expert in Serbia, speaking on condition of anonymity.

“Interference can lead to the collapse of transport, the failure of telecommunications networks, problems in banking systems, while emergency services lose the ability to locate incidents quickly.”

The protest Novak took photos of, in May, wasn’t the only one where jamming and spoofing were detected.

Data from GPSwise and GPSJam show both phenomena occurred between 1 p.m. and 5 p.m. on March 15, 2025, when Serbia witnessed one of the biggest anti-government protests in its history.

According to GPSwise data, fake satellite signals affected several commercial flights, including Pegasus Airlines flights from Paris to Istanbul, London to Istanbul and Amsterdam to Istanbul, a Smartwings Hungary flight from Budapest to Egypt, and Wizz Air flights from Catania, southern Italy, to Warsaw and from Brussels to Craiova, Romania.

A source with expertise in the civil aviation sector, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said pilots landing at Nikola Tesla Airport also reported navigation interference.

“What I know is that the largest number of problems coincided with March 15,” the source told BIRN. “That was when the highest number of reports came in. Five, six, seven aircraft reported problems – it was obvious that something was going on.”

One Wizz Air flight received false navigation data while it was still over Hungary, approximately 250 kilometres from the source of the interference in Belgrade.

The Pegasus flight from Paris to Istanbul was over Krupanj, some 100 kilometres southwest of Belgrade, when it encountered the same problem.

“Since GNSS signals are not selective, interfering with one drone also affects all other systems within a radius ranging from several hundred metres to several kilometres,” said the radio frequency and telecommunications expert. “Their disruption is justified only in extreme security situations.”

“The operational range of such systems can be quite extensive, and to maximise effectiveness, jamming systems generally operate at maximum transmitter power,”

“The aircraft detect lower-intensity interference because each directional jamming beam can still be detected at much lower intensity over considerable distances, particularly in airspace.”

The source with civil aviation expertise said that, while aircraft have other navigation systems, they “primarily rely on GNSS” when approaching airports.

“Today, pilots generally do not fly aircraft manually but rely on computers, whose most important requirement is to know the aircraft’s precise position at all times,” the source told BIRN.

“All major airports, including Belgrade, have precision approach procedures that require certain standards to be met, including reliable satellite navigation. Without it, that level of precision is significantly reduced.”

If navigation systems are disrupted, pilots are obliged to make a report, he said.

Drones grounded

World.title: Croatia Gets First Regular Beijing Air Connection as Air China Launches Zagreb Route
World.content:
July the 24th, 2026 – Croatia is set to get its first regular Beijing air connection as Air China launches a Beijing-Bucharest-Zagreb route.

Croatia is set to receive its first regular air link with the Chinese capital, Beijing, as Chinese national carrier Air China prepares to launch a new route connecting the two cities from September 2026.

Luka Fisic reports for Jutarnji that this new service will operate on the Beijing–Bucharest–Zagreb route, with the first flight scheduled for the 4th of September 2026. Flights will run three times per week, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays, using an Airbus A330-200 aircraft. Although the aircraft will make a stop in the Romanian capital of Bucharest, passengers travelling between Zagreb and Beijing will not actually need to change planes, making the journey significantly easier compared with current options that usually require connections through major European or Middle Eastern hubs.

stronger tourism and business connections between croatia and china

The new route is expected to strengthen tourism, business and cultural connections between Croatia and China. Beijing is one of Asia’s largest aviation hubs, meaning Croatian passengers will also gain easier access to further destinations across China and the wider region.

Ticket sales have already opened, with return fares reportedly starting at around 650 euros and reaching approximately 1,000 euros, depending on travel dates and availability. The basic fare also includes checked baggage, making the offer more attractive for long-distance travellers. The launch comes as Croatia continues to expand international air connectivity and attract visitors from new markets. China was previously one of Croatia’s important long-haul tourism markets before the coronavirus pandemic, and improved flight links could help bring more Chinese visitors back to Croatian destinations.

For Croatian travellers, the new Air China service represents a major milestone: for the first time, Zagreb will have a regular scheduled connection with Beijing, opening a direct gateway between Croatia and one of the world’s largest cities.

World.title: The Place in Croatia Where a 5000-Year-Old Revolution Began
World.content:
July the 24th, 2026 – There’s a place tucked away in eastern Croatia where a 5000-year-old revolution of sorts began. Few realise that this overlooked location became on of Europe’s most advanced centres long before Rome was built.

Many thousands of years before modern technology as we know it today completely transformed Europe, a prehistoric culture in what is now eastern Croatia was already pushing the boundaries of innovation of the time. On the banks of the Danube, near the Croatian hero city of Vukovar, the ancient settlement of Vučedol became one of Europe’s most advanced centres around 5,000 years ago.

The people who lived there, known as the ancient Vučedol culture, developed technologies and skills that were far ahead of their time. Putni kofer writes that they diligently constructed properly organised settlements, produced all kinds of advanced ceramics, worked with metal and created tools that influenced the development of later European societies.

the spread of knowledge…

One of their most famous achievements was metallurgy. The Vučedol people were among the first communities in all of Europe to master copper processing, marking a major transition from the Stone Age into the Copper Age. Their knowledge of metalworking helped shape a new era of technological development across the continent. Their innovations did not stop there. Archaeologists have discovered significant amounts of evidence that the Vučedol people had surprisingly sophisticated knowledge of astronomy. Their famous Orion calendar, often described as one of the oldest European calendars, shows that they carefully observed the movements of the stars and used that knowledge in everyday life.

LZMK

Their pottery was also totally unique. Vučedol ceramics featured distinctive decorations and shapes, including the famous Vučedol dove vessel, which has become one of the symbols of Croatia’s prehistoric heritage. These objects reveal a society with advanced artistic skills and a strong cultural identity. The settlement of Vučedol was so much more than another European prehistoric village, it was a centre of innovation at a time when the entire continent was undergoing major changes. Around 5,000 years ago, while many communities were still relying on traditional tools and methods, the Vučedol culture was experimenting with new technologies that would influence the future of the continent.

Today, the Vučedol Archaeological Site and Museum preserve the story of this remarkable civilisation, reminding visitors that some of Europe’s earliest technological breakthroughs happened right here in Croatia.

World.title: Croatia Airlines to Serve Authentic Dalmatian Flavours from August
World.content:
July the 24th, 2026 – Croatia Airlines is set to serve its passengers authentic Dalmatian flavours as of August the 1st this year.

Passengers flying on Croatia Airlines planes will be treated to a genuine taste of Dalmatia before they even land as the national carrier launches a new onboard gastronomic offer. Poslovni reports that as of August the 1st, Dalmatian flavours will be able to be enjoyed before the aircraft’s wheels even touch Croatian soil. The move is primarily designed to showcase this special region of Croatia’s local food producers and rich culinary traditions.

The new initiative is part of a collaboration between Croatia Airlines, the Split-Dalmatia County Tourist Board and the county itself. The aim is to introduce travellers to authentic Dalmatian products during their flight, creating a unique welcome experience while promoting this coastal region’s food, culture and local businesses.

Passengers will receive specially curated snack packages featuring a selection of products made by producers from the Split-Dalmatia region. The project is intended not only to enhance the in-flight experience but also to encourage visitors to explore local gastronomy once they arrive at their destination.

Those within tourism have claimed that food and drink have become an increasingly important part of the travel experience, with many visitors choosing destinations based on their culinary heritage. By bringing regional flavours on board, Croatia Airlines hopes to strengthen the connection between air travel and Croatia’s tourism offer while supporting local producers.

The programme follows similar regional collaborations introduced by the airline, which has already featured products from other Croatian destinations as part of its efforts to highlight the country’s diverse gastronomic heritage.

The new Dalmatian snack selection will be available on Croatia Airlines flights as of the first day of August, giving passengers an opportunity to sample a taste of one of Croatia’s most popular tourist regions before their holiday even begins.

World.title: Working From Home in Croatia Remains Rare Compared to Europe
World.content:
July the 24th, 2026 – Working from home boomed during the coronavirus pandemic, with the world altering tremendously in that regard, but it still remains rare in Croatia.

Working from home remains the exception rather than the rule across Croatia, with the country ranking near the bottom of the entire European Union for remote work despite the widespread adoption of flexible working models elsewhere across the continent.

According to the latest Eurostat data, only a small share of employed people in Croatia usually work from home, placing the country among the EU’s lowest-ranked nations. By comparison, countries such as Finland and Ireland have embraced remote work on a much larger scale, with around one in five employees regularly working from home. The EU average is close to 9 percent.

The figures highlight a growing divide between northern and southern Europe. While remote and hybrid work have become firmly established in many countries since the COVID-19 pandemic, Croatia has largely returned to traditional office-based working patterns. Analysts point out that the country’s economic structure plays a significant role, as many of Croatia’s largest industries—including tourism, hospitality, retail, construction and manufacturing—require employees to be physically present at work.

Another factor is company culture. Many Croatian employers continue to favour in-person work, particularly in small and medium-sized businesses where remote work policies have been slower to develop. Even in sectors where working from home is technically possible, employers often prefer office attendance over flexible arrangements.

The data also reflects how unevenly remote work has developed across Europe. Finland leads the bloc, followed by Ireland, while countries such as Romania, Bulgaria and Greece record the lowest shares. Croatia sits much closer to that group than to the EU average, underlining how limited remote work remains in the country.

Experts note that hybrid working is more common than the statistics suggest, as Eurostat’s methodology counts only people who usually work from home for at least half of their working time. Employees who occasionally work remotely but spend most of the week in the office are not included in the headline figures.

Although flexible working arrangements continue to expand across many parts of Europe, Croatia’s labour market remains heavily office- and workplace-based. Whether that changes in the coming years is likely to depend on employer attitudes, investment in digital jobs, and the continued growth of sectors where remote work is a practical option.

World.title: Europa League Qualifiers: Hajduk Beats Pafos 2-0 in First Leg
World.content:
Hajduk hosted Cyprus’s Pafos at Poljud tonight in the first leg of the Europa League second qualifying round. Having knocked out Slovakia’s Žilina in the first round, the Split side faced a tough task against a team that competed in the Champions League last season.

Should Gonzalo Garcia’s side get past Pafos, they’ll face Austria’s Salzburg in the third qualifying round, while the losing side drops into the Conference League third qualifying round, taking on the winner of the tie between Georgia’s Dinamo Tbilisi and Lithuania’s Žalgiris.

Lineups

Hajduk: Silić; Acapandie, Marešić, Van Hoorenbeeck, Hrgović — Pajaziti, Pukštas — Brajković, Dalisson, Melnjak — Šego

Pafos: Majecki; Mmaee, Luiz, Goldar — Ioannou, Šunjić, Pepe, Jaja — Gabriel Teixeira, Dragomir, Lele

Match report

Pafos threatened early on when Pajaziti lost the ball in midfield in the 4th minute and pulled back Teixeira to stop the counter, picking up the game’s first yellow card in the process.

Hajduk responded with a promising move in the 5th minute, as Šego laid the ball back to Melnjak, who left it for Hrgović, though Pafos managed to cut the move short before it could develop.

Hajduk had their first real sight of goal in the 8th minute, when a dangerous free-kick from Šego cannoned off the defensive wall and out for a corner.

Pafos threatened in the 15th minute, when a long-range free-kick was met by Goldar’s header, but Silić dealt with it comfortably. Hajduk’s early total dominance eased slightly by the 18th minute, when Pepe’s long-range effort drifted harmlessly over the bar.

Hrgović and Melnjak combined well down the left in the 21st minute to get in behind the Pafos defense, but Hrgović’s low ball into the middle failed to find a teammate.

The game grew more even by the 29th minute, though Pafos still hadn’t created a genuine chance of their own. Hajduk came desperately close in the 25th minute, when Melnjak whipped in a superb ball to the box for Šego, who was a fraction late arriving and couldn’t quite get enough on it to test the keeper.

Dalisson showed good feet between two defenders in the 31st minute, feeding the ball left to Hrgović, who curled an effort towards the far post from an angle — somewhere between a shot and a cross.

Poljud rang with whistles in the 35th minute after Dalisson went down under a challenge, followed by a foul awarded against Pajaziti in a similar situation moments later, with the Albanian, already on a yellow card, now needing to be careful.

Hajduk almost broke through again in the 41st minute, when Hrgović whipped in another sharp delivery from the left towards the far post, but Šego couldn’t quite connect with a sliding effort.

Pafos had a sight of goal in the 43rd minute, when Dragomir’s corner found David Luiz, but his header lacked any real danger.

Only one minute of stoppage time was played before the referee brought the first half to a close.

The second half got underway with no changes to either side.

Hajduk won a dangerous free-kick in the 55th minute when Ioannou fouled Brajković and was booked for his troubles, handing Hajduk a chance from a threatening position.

They made it count immediately. In the 56th minute, Šego stepped up to the resulting free-kick from around 20 meters and beat the Pafos goalkeeper with the aid of the crossbar — Hajduk led 1-0!

Pafos made a double change in the 62nd minute, with Pepe and Goldar making way for Brito and Bruno.

Hajduk doubled their lead just three minutes later. In the 65th minute, Acapandie and Dalisson combined with a slick one-two down the right, and Acapandie’s ball into the middle was turned home with a brilliant reaction finish from Melnjak’s left foot — 2-0 to Hajduk!

Pafos took the initiative in the 70th minute and pushed forward with everything they had, but Hajduk’s defense held firm.

Pafos made another double change in the 74th minute, with Šunjić and Dragomir replaced by Quina and Rodrigues.

Garcia responded with a triple substitution of his own in the 77th minute, bringing on Livaja, Skelin and Del Moral for Šego, Marešić and Dalisson — with Livaja’s introduction greeted by a thunderous ovation from the stands.

Huram replaced Melnjak in the 82nd minute. Hajduk’s defense continued to hold firm. Pafos pressed but had yet to fashion a genuine chance.

In the 87th minute, Huram received a yellow card.

Three minutes of stoppage time were added, and Pafos had one last chance with a free kick just outside the box, but it was an easy clear for Hajduk.



The game finished 2-0. The second leg is next Thursday, July 30th, in Paphos.

World.title: Croatian Tourism Season Holding Steady as July Matches 2025’s Pace
World.content:
July the 23rd, 2026 – The Croatian tourism season is doing well as July this year is so far matching July 2025’s pace.

As Istrain.hr reports, the tourism industry remains on track for another strong year, with July performing at roughly the same level as last year’s record season, according to Croatian National Tourist Board (HTZ) Director Kristjan Staničić.

Speaking after a coordination meeting with tourist boards from Zadar County, Staničić revealed that the season has unfolded largely as expected. While June saw a slight dip compared to 2025, that followed a particularly strong May, leaving overall results for the first six months of the year virtually unchanged from last year. Early figures for July suggest that the trend is continuing. Staničić stressed that every single tourist season is influenced by different factors, including school holiday schedules, economic conditions in Croatia’s key source markets and major international events. Despite those variables, he believes Croatia has maintained a stable position in an increasingly competitive Mediterranean market.

“there’s no stagnation”

He also rejected suggestions that Croatian tourism has entered a period of stagnation, pointing instead to the country’s long-term strategy of growing outside the peak summer months. Rather than relying solely on July and August, Croatia is continuing to invest in pre-season and post-season tourism through health tourism, congress tourism, improved destination experiences and stronger air connectivity.

A key priority remains expanding flight connections. HTZ has increased funding for strategic partnerships with airlines and tour operators by around 30 percent this year, with the aim of improving access to Croatia, particularly during the shoulder seasons. Officials are also encouraging regional tourist boards to work more closely with airlines as they begin planning routes for next year.

new private accommodation rules cause a stir

Staničić also defended recent government measures affecting private accommodation landlords, arguing they should be viewed as part of a long-term strategy to improve quality and tackle the grey economy rather than as short-term restrictions.

He highlighted the “Your Host” quality label, which has helped participating properties achieve higher occupancy rates and greater visibility, while noting that future legislative changes will introduce stricter oversight of unregistered accommodation.

With visitor numbers broadly matching last year’s record-breaking performance despite a more challenging international environment, Croatia’s tourism authorities remain optimistic that the country is on course for another successful season.

World.title: Budget Fashion Chain Primark Set to Open Its First Store in Croatia
World.content:
July the 23rd, 2026 – Budget fashion chain Primark, which is extremely popular in every country in which it operates, is set to open its very first store in Croatia. Until now, the closest was in Ljubljana.

One of Europe’s most popular affordable fashion retailers by far is finally heading to Croatia. Primark, the Irish clothing giant known for its low prices and trend-driven collections, is preparing to open its first Croatian store, marking a long-awaited arrival for many local shoppers. Poslovni reports that for very many years, Croatian customers have travelled to neighbouring countries such as Slovenia, Austria and Italy to shop at Primark stores, often returning with suitcases full of clothing, accessories and homeware. Soon, they will be able to do so without leaving the country.

Primark has built an incredibly loyal following across Europe by offering fashionable clothing, footwear, beauty products and home goods at highly competitive prices. Its arrival in Croatia has been the subject of speculation for years, fuelled by strong demand from shoppers who regularly visit stores abroad. Social media has also played a role in the retailer’s popularity, with fashion influencers frequently showcasing Primark’s latest collections and seasonal bargains.

the first croatian primark store will be near zagreb

According to reports, the retailer is preparing to open its first Croatian location at Designer Outlet Croatia in Rugvica, just outside Zagreb. The shopping centre has increasingly attracted international brands, and Primark’s arrival is expected to further strengthen its position as one of Croatia’s leading retail destinations. While an official opening date has yet to be announced, preparations are reportedly underway.

Unlike many international fashion retailers, Primark focuses on offering the latest trends at prices that are often significantly lower than competitors. Its stores are known for having everything in stock, from everyday basics and seasonal fashion to children’s clothing, cosmetics, home decor and licensed merchandise from popular films and television series. The combination of wide product selection and low prices has made Primark one of Europe’s fastest-growing fashion retailers.

a much needed boost for croatia’s expensive retail sector (and for the public’s wallets)

Primark’s arrival reflects Croatia’s growing attractiveness to international retail brands. As consumer spending continues to evolve and modern shopping centres expand their offerings, more global retailers are viewing the Croatian market as an increasingly attractive destination. The opening is also expected to reduce the need for Croatian shoppers to travel abroad specifically for Primark purchases, keeping more retail spending within the country.

For thousands of Croatian fashion enthusiasts, the news ends years of waiting. Instead of planning shopping trips across the border, customers will soon have access to one of Europe’s best-known budget fashion brands much closer to home. If the first store proves successful, it could also pave the way for additional Primark locations in other Croatian cities in the years ahead.

World.title: Estonian citizen in US pleads guilty to procuring electronics for Russia
World.content:
An Estonian citizen has pleaded guilty in a U.S. court to procuring sensitive electronics for the benefit of the Russian military for "nearly a decade" and faces up to 40 years' imprisonment.

The U.S. Attorney's Office said Estonian citizen Andrey Shevlyakov's scheme to evade export rules caused the illegal export of over $1 million worth of sensitive electronics from the United States.

Court documents show Shevlyakov was banned from acquiring any items from the United States without the Department of Commerce's permission, and he spent years evading U.S. export controls.

He was arrested by the Estonian authorities in 2023 and extradited to the U.S. in August 2025.

Guilty plea

On Thursday, he pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit export violations for his role in a procurement network that obtained sensitive electronics for the benefit of Russian military and government contractors, a statement from the U.S. Attorney's Office said.

Shevlyakov faces a maximum sentence of 40 years' imprisonment and has already agreed to forfeit approximately $1.5 million to the government.

"For nearly a decade, the defendant operated a foreign procurement network and supplied sophisticated U.S. technology to hostile Russian military actors, undermining U.S. national security and the security of our allies," stated United States Attorney Nocella.

"Today's guilty plea demonstrates that our Office will vigorously prosecute and hold to account those who aid Russian attempts to illegally procure U.S. technology, no matter who they are or where they reside."

FBI Houston Special Agent in Charge Hudson said Shevlyakov's arrest was the result of a spinoff case from a much larger FBI investigation that goes back some 14 years.

Shell companies and Russian customers

The U.S. Attorney's Office said Shevlyakov deceived U.S. manufacturers and suppliers and acquired sensitive technology and electronics by using multiple shell companies.

He then shipped the items to end-users in Russia, including defense contractors and Russian government agencies.

Shevlyakov was aware of his prohibited status but flouted U.S. export controls.

In one case, Shevlyakov placed an order with a U.S. company for sensitive electronic components, but the company refused to sell to the defendant and informed him he was on the Entity List. Shevlyakov then canceled his order, only to place it again days later using a different email address and under a false name.

The items he obtained for his Russian customers included low-noise pre-scalers and synthesizers used to conduct high-frequency communications.

He also obtained analog-to-digital converters, which are used in defense systems, including avionics, missiles, and electronic warfare systems.

He communicated extensively with Russian defense contractors and telecommunications companies about the sensitive items he procured.

Crossed the border over 100 times

Shevlyakov traveled extensively between Estonia and Russia to deliver the items he obtained.

International border crossing records for the period 2010-2016 show that during that period, Shevlyakov crossed the Estonian border and into Russia over 100 times, many times on same-day trips.

Records provided by the Finnish government show that the defendant was stopped by Finnish authorities while trying to smuggle electronics into Russia.

Shevlyakov failed to provide a customs declaration, and Finnish border guards searched the defendant's car and discovered approximately €70,000 worth of electronics hidden throughout the vehicle.

World.title: Estonian family's 300-animal hobby farm a labor of love
World.content:
Running a hobby farm may not make financial sense, but for Marili Põrk and her family, the rewards of their Northern Estonian farm far outweigh the costs.

Põrk, who owns Suureoja Farm in Harju County, said they care for nearly 300 animals while also juggling full-time work.

"Hobby farming means we're doing all of this on the side of our dayjobs," she explained. "Financially it doesn't pay off, but emotionally it absolutely does."

The farm began as a way for the parents to give their four kids, two of whom have since grown up, firsthand experience with rural life.

Today, Suureoja Farm is home to more than 250 sheep, beef cattle, Highland cattle, goats, geese, chickens, turkeys, rabbits, peacocks, cats and eight dogs.

"We do it all as a family, without hired help," the owner said.

Some days harder than others

Like many small-scale farmers, Põrk admits there are moments when the workload feels overwhelming, especially during haymaking season, lambing or when animals escape their enclosures.

She said the family has occasionally considered giving up farming, particularly after exhausting days, because they are ultimately responsible for live animals. But the thought never lasts long.

"Then we end up bringing home another animal, and then we're back to enjoying life again," Põrk added.

Suureoja Farm has welcomed visitors during Estonia's annual nationwide Open Farm Days for the past ten years and counting.

This year's Open Farm Days take place July 25–26.

World.title: Defense Intelligence: Strikes on online retail hubs add economic pressure on Russia
World.content:
Ukraine's successful airstrikes in Russia, whose newest targets in recent weeks have included warehouses of internet platforms, are significantly damaging the aggressor's economy, the Estonian Defense Intelligence Center says in its Friday overview.

"Such strikes amplify the deterioration of the business climate in Russia, and the index describing it fell in July to –3.6 points according to the Russian central bank — the lowest figure since mid‑2022. Although President Putin tried again this week to give the impression that Russia's economy is not doing too badly — in May the economy grew by 0.3 percent according to him — Ukraine's long‑range strikes are reshaping that reality," the intelligence center's weekly report states.

Over the past seven days, a new category of targets has been added to Ukraine's strikes: warehouses of the company Wildberries, which were attacked in Moscow and Tambov oblasts and in Krasnodar and Stavropol krais.

The latest such strikes occurred overnight near St. Petersburg.

Although Russia's largest online retail platform Wildberries is not directly a military enterprise, it mediates the sale of military equipment such as bulletproof vests and other protective gear, uniforms, drones and their components, and units of the Russian armed forces and supporting individuals buy all kinds of equipment from it.

"Wildberries and its competitor Ozon are used by a large part of Russia's population, and Ukraine's strikes therefore have a significant effect in addition to the direct economic damage, which may reach two billion dollars. The impact of Ukraine's strikes is illustrated by the fact that in 2025 the total value of goods sold by Wildberries equaled roughly three percent of the Russian Federation's gross domestic product (GDP)," noted Estonian military intelligence.
